'''Wilson:''' {{legend0|#FFC8CD|30–40%}} {{legend0|#FFB2B2|40–50%}} | title = [[Governor of Alaska|Governor]] | before_election = [[Mike Dunleavy (politician)|Mike Dunleavy]] | before_party = Alaska Republican Party | after_election = [[Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins]] | after_party = Alaska Democratic Party }} {{ElectionsAK}} The '''2026 Alaska gubernatorial election''' took place on November 3, 2026, to elect the next [[Governor of Alaska|governor]] and [[Lieutenant Governor of Alaska|lieutenant governor of Alaska]]. A nonpartisan [[top-four primary]] election occurred on August 18, 2026, in which four candidates advanced to a [[Ranked-choice voting in the United States|ranked-choice]] general election, held using [[instant-runoff voting]].{{cite web|title = Primary Election Information|url = https://www.elections.alaska.gov/Core/primaryelectioninformation.php|website = Alaska Division of Elections|access-date = 2024-12-15|quote = Primary elections are held on the third Tuesday in August of even numbered years.|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20220504030110/https://www.elections.alaska.gov/Core/primaryelectioninformation.php|archive-date = May 4, 2022|url-status = dead}} Incumbent governor [[Mike Dunleavy (politician)|Mike Dunleavy]] was term-limited and ineligible to seek a third consecutive term. Democratic former state representative [[Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins]] won the election with an outright majority in the first-choice vote, becoming the first Democrat to be elected governor of Alaska since [[Tony Knowles (politician)|Tony Knowles]] in [[1998 Alaska gubernatorial election|1998]].{{Cite AV media |url=https://edition.cnn.com/2026/11/12/politics/video/democrats-pick-up-win-in-alaska-after-midterms-shellacking-for-gop-lcl |title=Democrats pick up win in Alaska after midterms shellacking for GOP {{!}} CNN Politics |language=en |access-date=2026-11-13}} Kreiss-Tomkins is only the third [[List of governors of Alaska|Governor of Alaska]] to be born in the state (after [[William A. Egan]] and [[Bill Walker (American politician)|Bill Walker]]), and the first to be born in the state after it achieved statehood. ==Candidates== === Republican Party === ==== Advanced to general ==== Candidates at times struggled to distinguish themselves, while Alaska's [[Nonpartisan primary#Alaska|nonpartisan primary]] and [[Ranked-choice voting in the United States#Alaska, 2022–present|ranked-choice voting]] system were credited with encouraging more positive campaigning. As a result, candidates often emphasized areas of agreement, particularly with members of their own party.{{cite news |last1=Samuels |first1=Iris |title=In Alaska’s crowded race for governor, candidates struggle to stand out as primary nears |url=https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/08/08/in-alaskas-crowded-race-for-governor-candidates-struggle-to-stand-out/ |access-date=August 21, 2026 |work=[[Anchorage Daily News]] |date=August 9, 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260810164447/https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/08/08/in-alaskas-crowded-race-for-governor-candidates-struggle-to-stand-out/ |archive-date=August 10, 2026 |url-status=live}} Republican Bernadette Wilson called on Republican candidates to withdraw if they advanced to the general election but received fewer votes than another Republican, though she was the only candidate to pledge to do so herself. Democrats [[Tom Begich]] and [[Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins]] similarly discussed the possibility of one withdrawing after the primary to consolidate Democratic support behind the other.{{cite news |last1=Brooks |first1=James |title=After Alaska’s ‘final four’ primary, a silent primary may decide who’s on the ballot in November |url=https://alaskabeacon.com/2026/08/14/after-alaskas-final-four-primary-a-silent-primary-may-decide-whos-on-the-ballot-in-november/ |access-date=August 21, 2026 |work=[[Alaska Beacon]] |date=August 14, 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260818213201/https://alaskabeacon.com/2026/08/14/after-alaskas-final-four-primary-a-silent-primary-may-decide-whos-on-the-ballot-in-november/ |archive-date=August 18, 2026 |url-status=live}} The race also saw heavy spending. Republicans [[Treg Taylor]] and Matt Heilala, the party's two highest-spending candidates, largely self-funded their campaigns. Heilala contributed $1.4 million to his campaign, while Taylor contributed $600,000. Taylor's contribution violated an Alaska campaign finance deadline, though he argued that the restriction was unconstitutional. Kreiss-Tomkins spent more than any other candidate and reported the largest number of individual Alaskan contributors, although most of his funding came from outside the state, including employees of [[Anthropic]] and others connected to the artificial intelligence industry. Begich raised approximately $1.2 million, more than half of which came from two wealthy Alaskan donors.{{cite news |last1=Samuels |first1=Iris |title=Candidates in Alaska’s open governor’s race spend However, the Alaska Public Offices Commission recommended against certifying Taylor's candidacy after finding that his financial disclosure did not substantially comply with state law.{{cite news |last1=Samuels |first1=Iris |date=August 28, 2026 |title=Alaska campaign watchdog says Treg Taylor should not be allowed to run for governor |url=https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/08/28/alaska-campaign-watchdog-says-treg-taylor-should-not-be-allowed-to-run-for-governor/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260829081050/https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/08/28/alaska-campaign-watchdog-says-treg-taylor-should-not-be-allowed-to-run-for-governor/ |archive-date=August 29, 2026 |access-date=August 29, 2026 |work=[[Anchorage Daily News]]}} On August 31, [[Lieutenant Governor of Alaska|Lieutenant Governor]] [[Nancy Dahlstrom]] declined to certify Taylor, temporarily elevating his running mate, Candice English, to the gubernatorial nomination; English subsequently selected Taylor's wife, Jodi Taylor, as her running mate.{{cite web |last=Samuels |first=Iris |date=August 31, 2026 |title=Treg Taylor disqualified from ballot as pressure grows for consolidated governor’s race |url=https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/08/31/pressure-grows-for-a-consolidated-gop-field-in-alaska-governors-race-as-deadline-nears/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260831200254/https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/08/31/pressure-grows-for-a-consolidated-gop-field-in-alaska-governors-race-as-deadline-nears/ |archive-date=August 31, 2026 |work=[[Anchorage Daily News]]}} On September 4, Dahlstrom reversed her decision and announced that Taylor would be certified after a preliminary review by the Alaska Department of Law raised questions about whether the financial disclosure requirements had been applied consistently.{{Cite web |last=Samuels |first=Iris |title=Treg Taylor is back in Alaska’s race for governor after election officials reverse decision |url=https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/09/04/treg-taylor-is-back-in-alaskas-race-for-governor-after-election-officials-reverse-decision/ |access-date=2026-09-05 |website=Anchorage Daily News}} In the general election campaign, Taylor softened his messaging and attempted to appeal to independent and Democratic voters. Kreiss-Tomkins pledged that Democrats, Republicans, and independents would be equally represented in his cabinet and emphasized endorsements from [[Moderate Republicans (modern United States)|moderate Republicans]]. In contrast, Wilson criticized [[Bipartisanship in United States politics|bipartisanship]] and said that bipartisan coalitions in the [[Alaska legislature]] had been ineffective.{{cite news |last1=Samuels |first1=Iris |title=Heeding ranked choice voting, candidates refine their strategies in Alaska governor’s race |url=https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/09/16/heeding-ranked-choice-voting-candidates-refine-their-strategies-in-alaska-governors-race/ |access-date=September 18, 2026 |work=[[Anchorage Daily News]] |date=September 17, 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260917151432/https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/09/16/heeding-ranked-choice-voting-candidates-refine-their-strategies-in-alaska-governors-race/ |archive-date=September 17, 2026 |url-status=live}} Taylor and Bronson called upon Republican voters to rank all three Republicans in the race, while Wilson urged her supporters not to rank other candidates and renewed her calls for the other Republicans to drop out.{{cite news |last1=Samuels |first1=Iris |title=Wilson again calls on her Republican opponents to drop out of Alaska governor’s race |url=https://www.adn.com/politics/2026/09/18/wilson-again-calls-on-her-republican-opponents-to-drop-out-of-alaska-governors-race/ |access-date=September 19, 2026 |work=[[Anchorage Daily News]] |date=September 18, 2026}} While the three Republican candidates generally agreed on most issues, including opposition to new taxation proposals from Kreiss-Tomkins, Wilson was alone in advocating for a return to paying out full [[Permanent Fund Dividend|Permanent Fund dividends]] according to the statutory formula. Incumbent governor [[Mike Dunleavy (politician)|Mike Dunleavy]] had made a similar promise during his [[2018 Alaska gubernatorial election|2018]] campaign, but his efforts to implement the proposal had been unsuccessful. In fact, dividends reached a record low during Dunleavy's administration. The other candidates argued that following the statutory formula would be unaffordable for the foreseeable future. The candidates also diverged on the issue of [[Data center|data centers]]. Bronson and Taylor were generally supportive of data centers, portraying them as an economic opportunity provided they generated their own electricity and did not drive up energy costs. Despite receiving large campaign contributions from donors connected to the artificial intelligence industry, Kreiss-Tomkins advocated for a moratorium on data center construction until a regulatory framework could be developed. He also supported regulation of artificial intelligence more broadly. Wilson also opposed data centers, highlighting their environmental impact and arguing that Kreiss-Tomkins could not be trusted on the issue.{{cite news |last1=Brooks |first1=James |title=Where do [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] senator [[Tommy Tuberville]] and [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] former senator [[Doug Jones (politician)|Doug Jones]] were the nominees for their respective parties. Republican incumbent [[Kay Ivey]] was [[Term limits in the United States|term-limited]] and ineligible to seek a third full consecutive term. [[Primary elections]] were held on May 19, 2026.{{cite web |title=Alabama Election Cycle Calendar |url=https://www.sos.alabama.gov/sites/default/files/2025-06/Alabama%20Election%20Chart%202026-2036%206.12.2025.pdf |website=Alabama Secretary of State |access-date=21 March 2025}} This was a rematch of the [[2020 United States Senate election in Alabama|2020 Senate election]], where Tuberville defeated incumbent senator Jones. Democrats have not won a gubernatorial election in Alabama since [[1998 Alabama gubernatorial election|1998]]. On November 3, 2026, Tuberville was declared the winner by the [[Associated Press]]. He won 51% to Jones's 47%, making it the closest gubernatorial election in Alabama since [[2002 Alabama gubernatorial election|2002]].{{Cite news |last=Zhang |first=Christine |last2=Wagner The governor and lieutenant governor shall each be at least thirty years of age when elected, and shall have been citizens of the United States ten years and resident citizens of this state at least seven years next before the date of their election.{{Cite web|title=SECTION 117|url=https://law.justia.com/constitution/alabama/CA-245654.html|access-date=January 30, 2026|website=[[Justia]]}}
Throughout Tuberville's gubernatorial campaign, many alleged that he did not satisfy the seven-year residency condition, which would have rendered him ineligible to hold the office. === Background === [[File:Map of Alabama and Florida with Lee County, AL and Walton County, FL highlighted.png|thumb|Tuberville owns residences in Lee County, Alabama, and Walton County, Florida.]] Tuberville is originally from Arkansas. In addition to his 9-year tenure at [[Auburn University]] in Alabama, Tuberville's football coaching career variously placed him in Florida, Mississippi, Texas, and Ohio.{{Cite news |last=Brassil |first=Gillian R. |date=2020-07-15 |title=Tuberville Advances: Will Alabama Send an Auburn Coach to the Senate? |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/07/15/sports/tommy-tuberville-alabama-auburn.html |access-date=2026-07-09 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} In July 2017, having retired from coaching and joined [[ESPN]] as an analyst, Tuberville recorded a promotional video at his residence in [[Santa Rosa Beach, Florida]], in which he says, "Six months ago, after 40 years of coaching football, I hung up my whistle and moved to Santa Rosa Beach, Florida, with the white sands and the blue water. What a great place to live."{{Cite web |last=Volner |first=Derek |date=2017-07-19 |title=Greetings from the beach: New ESPN, ABC CFB analyst Tommy Tuberville |url=https://www.espnfrontrow.com/2017/07/greetings-beach-new-espn-abc-cfb-analyst-tommy-tuberville/ |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=ESPN Front Row |language=en-US}} Tuberville purchased the 4,000-square-foot Florida residence through an [[Limited liability company|LLC]] in 2004,{{Cite news |last=Hakim |first=Danny |date=2020-10-12 |title=Tommy Tuberville’s Financial Fumbles |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/10/12/us/elections/senate-alabama-tuberville-jones.html |access-date=2026-07-09 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} and its value was estimated at $5.6 million in 2026.{{Cite web |last=Press |first=Associated |date=2026-06-14 |title=Tuberville residency hearing today in Hoover |url=https://aldailynews.com/tuberville-residency-hearing-today-in-hoover/ |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=Alabama Daily News |language=en-US}} In March 2017, Tuberville filed preliminary paperwork to run for governor of Alabama in the [[2018 Alabama gubernatorial election|2018 election]],{{Cite web |last=Stevens |first=Matthew |title=Tuberville files paperwork & receives $100K loan for potential governor run |url=https://www.montgomeryadvertiser.com/story/news/2017/03/31/tuberville-files-paperwork-receives-100k-loan-potential-governor-run/99890632/ |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=Montgomery Advertiser |language=en-US}} but he withdrew less than a month later, citing the seven-year residency requirement as a concern.{{Cite web |last=Rapp |first=Timothy |title=Former Auburn HC Tommy Tuberville Announces He Will Not Run for Alabama Governor |url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/2705689-former-auburn-hc-tommy-tuberville-announces-he-will-not-run-for-alabama-governor |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=bleacherreport.com |language=en}} Tuberville was issued an Alabama driver's license in March 2019, shortly before declaring his candidacy in [[2020 United States Senate election in Alabama|the state's 2020 U.S. Senate race]].{{Cite web |last=Knowles |first=Sawyer |date=2026-06-15 |title=Alabama Republican Party rules that Tuberville fully meets residency requirements |url=https://256today.com/alabama-republican-party-rules-that-tuberville-fully-meets-residency-requirements/ |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=256 Today |language=en-US}} During the campaign, Tuberville claimed that he had moved to Alabama in August 2018, despite having voted in Florida in the [[2018 United States elections|November 2018 midterm elections]].{{Cite web |last=Jackson |first=Dale |date=2019-05-02 |title=Tuberville moved to Alabama to run for Senate in August 2018 -- but voted in Florida in last November's election |url=https://yellowhammernews.com/tuberville-moved-to-alabama-to-run-for-senate-in-august-2018-but-voted-in-florida-in-last-novembers-election/ |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=Yellowhammer News |language=en-US}} Tuberville cited a 1,551-square-foot home on Cherry Street in [[Auburn, Alabama]], as his primary residence.{{Cite web |last=jsharp@al.com |first=John Sharp {{!}} |date=2025-03-26 |title=Tommy Tuberville not the first to raise election residency questions: Do Alabama voters care? |url=https://www.al.com/politics/2025/03/tommy-tuberville-not-the-first-to-raise-election-residency-questions-do-alabama-voters-care.html |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=al |language=en}} The home was purchased under the names of Tuberville's wife and son in March 2017, and they claimed a [[homestead exemption]] in October 2018.{{Cite web |last=Sell |first=Mary |date=2025-04-29 |title=Tax records show Tuberville's Auburn homestead exemption since 2018 |url=https://aldailynews.com/tax-records-show-tubervilles-auburn-homestead-exemption-since-2018/ |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=Alabama Daily News |language=en-US}} Tuberville did not appear on the deed for the property himself until 2024.{{Cite web |last=Moon |first=Josh |date=2026-06-17 |title=The first, and most daunting, legal challenge to Tuberville's candidacy has been filed |url=https://www.alreporter.com/2026/06/17/the-first-and-most-daunting-legal-challenge-to-tubervilles-candidacy-has-been-filed/ |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=Alabama Political Reporter |language=en-US}} During the 2020 Republican primary for U.S. Senate, Republican opponent [[Bradley Byrne]] said of Tuberville, "We don't like [[Carpetbagger (politics)|carpetbaggers]] in Alabama,"{{Cite web |last=Poor |first=Jeff |date=2019-05-04 |title=Byrne on Tuberville's Florida voter registration: 'We don't like carpetbaggers in Alabama' |url=https://yellowhammernews.com/byrne-on-tubervilles-florida-voter-registration-we-dont-like-carpetbaggers-in-alabama/ |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=Yellowhammer News |language=en-US}} to which Tuberville commented at an August 2019 campaign event, "I'm not an everyday resident of Alabama. [...] I've been here most of the last 20 years. I've had property. So, you'll see that on TV – 'He's a carpetbagger.' Yeah, I'm a carpetbagger of this country. I love this country. I love this state. I'm a carpetbagger."{{Cite web |last=Poor |first=Jeff |date=2019-08-04 |title=Tuberville dings Trump for veterans' health care problems, addresses 'carpetbagger' label, tax dodging allegations in Shoals appearances |url=https://yellowhammernews.com/tuberville-dings-trump-for-veterans-health-care-problems-addresses-carpetbagger-label-tax-dodging-allegations-in-shoals-appearances/ |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=Yellowhammer News |language=en-US}} Republican primary opponent [[Jeff Sessions]] commissioned advertisements labeling Tuberville a "[[Florida Man]]"{{Cite web |last=Lesniewski |first=Niels |date=2020-03-06 |title=Jeff Sessions’ campaign calls Tuberville a ‘Florida man’ |url=https://rollcall.com/2020/03/06/jeff-sessions-campaign-calls-tuberville-a-florida-man/ |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=Roll Call |language=en-US}} and referred to him as a "tourist from Florida."{{Cite web |url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-attacks-sessions-ahead-of-senate-primary-runoff |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=www.pbs.org|title=Trump attacks Sessions ahead of Senate primary runoff|date=2020-03-04|last=Chandler|first=Kim}} In March 2025, amid speculation that Tuberville would mount a gubernatorial bid, Alabama state senator [[Sam Givhan]], a Republican, expressed concerns about Tuberville's ability to meet the residency requirement, saying during a radio appearance, "Owning a house in Alabama is not enough. You've got to live here seven years. [...] So that's going to be a hurdle."{{Cite web |last=Cason |first=Mike |date=2025-03-18 |title=Can Tuberville run for governor? Alabama Republican questions whether he meets residency requirement |url=https://www.al.com/politics/2025/03/can-tuberville-run-for-governor-alabama-republican-questions-whether-he-meets-residency-requirement.html |access-date=2026-07-15 |website=al |language=en}} During Tuberville's tenure as Senator, expense records have shown significant spending on air travel, transportation, and dining in the area near his Florida property.{{Cite web |last=Britt |first=Bill |date=2025-04-24 |title=Tuberville’s travel trail points to home in Florida, not Alabama |url=https://www.alreporter.com/2025/04/24/tubervilles-travel-trail-points-to-home-in-florida-not-alabama/ |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=Alabama Political Reporter |language=en-US}} In May 2026, speaking to reporters after his induction into the [[Alabama Sports Hall of Fame]], Tuberville said, "I go back to Auburn three or four ball games a year. Actually, I live in Auburn, but living mostly in [[Washington, D.C.|D.C]]., you know, during the week."{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iPdiCn7lUl4 |title=Alabama Sports Hall of Fame interviews: Tommy Tuberville |date=2026-05-08 |last=ABC 33/40 |access-date=2026-07-10 |via=YouTube}} === Challenges from Ken McFeeters === On January 27, 2026, after the filing deadline for the Republican Party primary had passed, Tuberville's gubernatorial primary opponent, Ken McFeeters, submitted a challenge to the [[Alabama Republican Party]], formally alleging that Tuberville did not satisfy the state's residency requirement. McFeeters alleged in his petition that Tuberville primarily resides at his beachfront house in Santa Rosa Beach, Florida.{{Cite web|author=NBC 15|title=Tuberville's Alabama residency formally challenged by gubernatorial opponent|url=https://mynbc15.com/news/local/tubervilles-alabama-residency-questioned-gop-urged-to-decide-on-eligibility|date=January 27, 2026|access-date=January 30, 2026|website=[[WMTV]]}} A spokesperson for Tuberville described the challenge as "a ridiculous PR stunt from a desperate candidate,"{{Cite web|last1=Davis|first1=Kayla|title=Republican candidate challenges Sen. Tommy Tuberville's residency, saying he lives in Florida|url=https://www.wvtm13.com/article/tuberville-mcfeeter-senator-alabama-governor-election/70176207|date=January 28, 2026|access-date=January 30, 2026|website=[[WVTM]]}} and Tuberville dismissed the allegation, stating, "What a joke. I guess they think, you know, I hadn't done my homework."{{Cite web|last1=Conlon|first1=Riley|last2=Higdon|first2=Michal|title='What a joke': Sen. Tommy Tuberville dismisses challenge to his Alabama residency|url=https://www.wvtm13.com/article/tuberville-residency-governor-challenge-alabama-florida/70193402|date=January 29, 2026|access-date=January 30, 2026|website=[[WVTM]]}} The Alabama Republican Party's 21-member steering committee reviewed the challenge on February 2, 2026, and rejected it, clearing the path for Tuberville to be on the primary ballot.{{cite web |last1=Marie Fogel |first1=Apryl |title=ALGOP steering committee votes down Tuberville, Wahl ballot challenges |url=https://1819news.com/news/item/algop-steering-committee-votes-down-tuberville-wahl-ballot-challenges |website=1819 News |access-date=2 February 2026 |date=February 2, 2026}} In a press release following the committee's decision, Tuberville's campaign chairman Jordan Doufexis celebrated that "common sense has prevailed and this made-up 'residency' hoax will be put to bed for good."{{Cite web |last=Press |first=Coach Tuberville |date=2026-02-02 |title=ALGOP Unanimously Votes to Dismiss Ridiculous "Residency" Challenge Against Coach Tuberville |url=https://www.coachforgovernor.com/post/algop-unanimously-votes-to-dismiss-ridiculous-residency-challenge-against-coach-tuberville |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=Coach Tommy Tuberville for Governor |language=en}} In March 2026, McFeeters announced on the steps of the [[Alabama State Capitol|Alabama Capitol]] that he had filed a lawsuit against Tuberville in the [[Covington County, Alabama|Covington County]] Circuit Court.{{Cite web |last=Chapoco |first=Ralph |date=2026-03-24 |title=Republican gubernatorial candidate files lawsuit against U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville |url=https://alabamareflector.com/2026/03/24/republican-gubernatorial-candidate-files-lawsuit-against-u-s-sen-tommy-tuberville/ |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=Alabama Reflector |language=en-US}} McFeeters, though not a lawyer, litigated the case ''[[Pro se legal representation in the United States|pro se]]'' and listed “God’s Law Team” as his law firm in the complaint.PLAINTIFF’S RESPONSE IN OPPOSITION TO DEFENDANT TUBERVILLE’S MOTION TO DISMISS AND MOTION FOR THRESHOLD DETERMINATION OF CONSTITUTIONAL ELIGIBILITYhttps://bloximages.chicago2.vip.townnews.com/lagniappemobile.com/content/tncms/assets/v3/editorial/c/1e/c1e5cf02-ffb6-499b-a514-fd3140bd74ce/6a0c7e77a1d9f.pdf.pdf{{Cite web |last=Chapoco |first=Ralph |date=2026-03-24 |title=Republican gubernatorial candidate files lawsuit against U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville |url=https://alabamareflector.com/2026/03/24/republican-gubernatorial-candidate-files-lawsuit-against-u-s-sen-tommy-tuberville/ |access-date=2026-07-10 |website=Alabama Reflector |language=en-US}} McFeeters pledged that he would drop out of the race if Tuberville released records demonstrating proof of residency.{{Cite web |last=Harrison |first=Claire |date=2026-03-25 |title=McFeeters files lawsuit challenging Tuberville’s residency |url=https://aldailynews.com/mcfeeters-files-lawsuit-challenging-tubervilles-residencyr/ |access-date=2026-07-15 |website=Alabama Daily News |language=en-US}} Tuberville did not release any records, and the lawsuit was dismissed for improper venue on May 18, 2026, the day before the primary election.{{Cite web |last=Chapoco |first=Ralph |date=2026-05-20 |title=Judge dismisses lawsuit challenging Tommy Tuberville's eligibility to be governor |url=https://alabamareflector.com/2026/05/19/judge-dismisses-lawsuit-challenging-tommy-tubervilles-eligibility-to-be-governor/ |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=Alabama Reflector |language=en-US}} On May 27, 2026, the week after the primary election, McFeeters filed another challenge with the Alabama Republican Party, arguing that the party should void Tuberville's nomination on eligibility grounds.{{Cite web |last=JOHNSON |first=SCOTT |date=2026-05-27 |title=Candidate seeks to void Tuberville nomination |url=https://www.lagniappemobile.com/news/alabama/election_2026/candidate-seeks-to-void-tuberville-nomination/article_eeee2816-55e1-499c-88d1-e9994197cacd.html |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=Lagniappe Daily |language=en}} The party's Candidate Committee voted to proceed with the contest, surprising McFeeters, who said he was "totally shocked."{{Cite web |last=JOHNSON |first=SCOTT |date=2026-06-01 |title=ALGOP advances Tuberville nomination challenge |url=https://www.lagniappemobile.com/news/alabama/algop-advances-tuberville-nomination-challenge/article_ce1da93a-071a-4c52-9cd5-d0fe5b246228.html |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=Lagniappe Daily |language=en}} During the proceedings, Tuberville produced seven years of heavily redacted Alabama tax returns, from 2018 to 2024.{{Cite web |last=Barrett |first=Anna |date=2026-06-02 |title=Tuberville submits income tax returns, expert says it's not enough to prove residency |url=https://alabamareflector.com/2026/06/02/tuberville-submits-income-tax-returns-expert-says-its-not-enough-to-prove-residency/ |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=Alabama Reflector |language=en-US}} However, by failing to adequately redact scannable [[PDF417|PDF417 barcodes]] in the corners of the document, the unredacted contents of the tax returns were inadvertently made available to the involved parties.{{Cite web |last=JOHNSON |first=SCOTT |date=2026-06-05 |title=Campaign exposes Tuberville’s tax, financial history |url=https://www.lagniappemobile.com/news/alabama/campaign-exposes-tuberville-s-tax-financial-history/article_578d2e17-d57a-4863-8682-3e3b65fe9a3a.html |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=Lagniappe Daily |language=en}} McFeeters, unconvinced that the tax returns sufficiently demonstrated proof of residency, shared plans to continue his challenge, telling [[AL.com]], "I want his wife to tell me, with a straight face, that she lives in a one-bathroom house with her husband and adults and guests. A woman like that is not going to share a bathroom."{{Cite web |last=Smith |first=Ruth Serven |date=2026-06-02 |title=Tuberville releases long-awaited tax returns, says he’s lived in Alabama since 2018 |url=https://www.al.com/news/2026/06/tuberville-releases-long-awaited-tax-returns-says-hes-lived-in-alabama-since-2018.html |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=al |language=en}} Following an internal closed-door hearing on June 14, 2026, the Alabama Republican Party Candidate Committee unanimously dismissed the challenge.{{Cite web |last=Knowles |first=Sawyer |date=2026-06-15 |title=Alabama Republican Party rules that Tuberville fully meets residency requirements |url=https://256today.com/alabama-republican-party-rules-that-tuberville-fully-meets-residency-requirements/ |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=256 Today |language=en-US}} In July 2026, McFeeters filed a second lawsuit with similar allegations in the [[Jefferson County, Alabama|Jefferson County]] Circuit Court.{{Cite web |last=Shelley |first=Jonathan |date=July 30, 2026 |title=Back to court: Ken McFeeters sues (again) over Tuberville's residency, eligibility for governor |url=https://www.rocketcitynow.com/article/news/state/back-to-court-ken-mcfeeters-sues-again-over-tubervilles-residency-eligibility-for-governor/525-4cec25e8-bc59-4143-9721-479fa17644dc}} The case was dismissed on August 18, 2026 for lack of jurisdiction.{{Cite web |last=Moon |first=Josh |date=2026-08-20 |title=Another Tuberville residency challenge has been dismissed |url=https://www.alreporter.com/2026/08/20/another-tuberville-residency-challenge-has-been-dismissed/ |access-date=2026-08-20 |website=Alabama Political Reporter |language=en-US}} On August 13, 2026, McFeeters additionally filed a federal lawsuit, which was dismissed one day later for lack of [[Standing (law)|standing]].{{Cite web |last=Shelley |first=Jonathan |date=August 14, 2026 |title=Judge dismisses federal lawsuit seeking to block Sen. Tuberville's run for governor |url=https://www.rocketcitynow.com/article/news/local/judge-dismisses-federal-lawsuit-seeking-to-block-sen-tubervilles-run-for-governor/525-dca50942-69d5-43d0-85b6-dc0f2678ce49}} === Quo warranto lawsuit === [[File:Barry Ragsdale - Anna Barrett, Alabama Reflector.jpg|thumb|219x219px|Birmingham lawyer Barry Ragsdale is an attorney for the plaintiffs.]] On June 17, 2026, plaintiffs Brook Dorgan and Justin LeBlanc filed a lawsuit against Tuberville in the [[Montgomery County, Alabama|Montgomery County]] Circuit Court, which seeks a [[Quo warranto|writ of ''quo warranto'']] to invalidate Tuberville's candidacy. The complaint, citing voter registration records, tax records, campaign finance records, and quotes from Tuberville himself, alleges that Tuberville has not consistently maintained residence at his Auburn, Alabama property.{{Cite web |title=EXPEDITED COMPLAINT FOR QUO WARRANTO AND DECLARATORY RELIEF |url=https://whnt.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2026/06/Tuberville-Residency-Challenge-Lawsuit.pdf}} The complaint requested an expedited jury trial, with plaintiffs' attorney Barry Ragsdale saying on a podcast, "We think that your average person who sits on a jury is just never, ever going to believe the stories that Tuberville makes up about where he lives."{{Cite web |title=Barry Ragsdale on the Tuberville Lawsuit |url=https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/barry-ragsdale-on-the-tuberville-lawsuit/id1845915473?i=1000774023089 |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=Apple Podcasts |language=en-US}} Tuberville filed a motion to dismiss the suit on June 22, 2026.{{Cite web |last=Harrison |first=Claire |date=2026-06-23 |title=Tuberville files motion to dismiss in latest residency case |url=https://aldailynews.com/tuberville-files-motion-to-dismiss-in-latest-residency-case/ |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=Alabama Daily News |language=en-US}} On July 9, 2026, Montgomery County Circuit Judge Brooke Reid dismissed the lawsuit for insufficient jurisdiction.{{Cite web |last=Barrett |first=Anna |date=2026-07-09 |title=Tommy Tuberville residency lawsuit dismissed by Montgomery judge |url=https://alabamareflector.com/2026/07/09/tommy-tuberville-residency-lawsuit-dismissed-by-montgomery-judge/ |access-date=2026-07-09 |website=Alabama Reflector |language=en-US}} The dismissal order cites a lack of case law concerning whether ''quo warranto'' may be applied for party nominees. However, Reid did affirm that the state constitution allows the judiciary to determine whether an individual satisfies the "clearly set forth and unambiguous" requirements to hold office, which Tuberville's lawyers had disputed. Reid did not render a verdict on the underlying question of Tuberville's eligibility. On July 14, 2026, Ragsdale filed an appeal to the [[Supreme Court of Alabama|Alabama Supreme Court]].{{Cite web |title=Barry Ragsdale appeals dismissed lawsuit challenging Tuberville’s… |url=https://1819news.com/news/item/barry-ragsdale-appeals-dismissed-lawsuit-challenging-tubervilles-residency-to-alabama-supreme-court |access-date=2026-07-14 |website=[[1819 News]] |language=en-US}} The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal in a 7–0 ruling.{{Cite web |title=Alabama Supreme Court rules 7-0 for Tuberville, ends ‘residency hoax’ in courts for good |url=https://yellowhammernews.com/alabama-supreme-court-rules-7-0-for-tuberville-ends-residency-hoax-in-courts-for-good/ |access-date=2026-10-09 |website=[[Yellowhammer News]] |language=en-US}} == See also == *[[2026 United States elections]] *[[2026 Alabama elections]] ==Notes== {{notelist}} '''Partisan clients'''

'''Tie:''' {{legend0|#DECDE6|30–40%}} {{legend0|#D2B1D9|40–50%}} {{legend0|#AE8BB1|50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No votes}} | title = [[Governor of Arkansas|Governor]] | before_election = [[Sarah Huckabee Sanders]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Sarah Huckabee Sanders]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsAR}} The '''2026 Arkansas gubernatorial election''' was held on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Arkansas]]. [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] incumbent [[Sarah Huckabee Sanders]] was re-elected to second term. She was challenged by [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] state senator [[Fredrick Love]] and [[Libertarian Party (United States)|Libertarian]] Colt Shelby. [[Primary elections]] took place on March 3, 2026. Huckabee Sanders secured the Republican nomination unopposed. Love defeated businesswoman Supha Xayprasith-Mays in the Democratic primary with 81.0% of the vote. Colt Shelby became the first third-party gubernatorial candidate since [[1896 Arkansas gubernatorial election|1896]] to win a plurality of the vote in an Arkansan county in his home county of [[Franklin County, Arkansas|Franklin]].{{cite news |title=Colt Shelby wins county as third party candidate in Arkansas for first time since 1800s |url=https://www.5newsonline.com/video/news/politics/elections/colt-shelby-wins-county-as-third-party-candidate-in-arkansas-for-first-time-since-1800s/527-0d29a6e8-bb3b-45a8-a893-532ca6d318fc |access-date=4 November 2026 |work=5newsonline.com |date=4 November 2026}} ==Republican primary== ===Candidates=== ====Nominee==== *[[Sarah Huckabee Sanders]], incumbent governor (2023–present){{Cite web|date=March 3, 2026|title=Arkansas Governor Primary Results 2026|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-primary-elections/arkansas-governor-results|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260717192937/https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-primary-elections/arkansas-governor-results|archive-date=July 17, 2026|access-date=August 6, 2026|work=[[NBC News]]}} ===Endorsements=== {{Endorsements box|title=Sarah Huckabee Sanders|list=;Executive branch officials *[[Donald Trump]], [[president of the United States]] (2017–2021, 2025–present){{Cite web|last=Roberts|first=Adams|date=November 3, 2025|title=President Donald Trump endorses Gov. 2026 Arizona gubernatorial election.text:
{{short description|none}} {{for|related races|2026 United States gubernatorial elections}} {{Use American English|date=January 2025}} {{use mdy dates|date=September 2023}} {{Infobox election | election_name = 2026 Arizona gubernatorial election | country = Arizona | type = presidential | ongoing = no | last_update = 10:30 AM | time_zone = [[Mountain Standard Time|MST]] | previous_election = 2022 Arizona gubernatorial election | previous_year = 2022 | next_election = 2030 Arizona gubernatorial election | next_year = 2030 | election_date = November 3, 2026 | image1 = Katie Hobbs 2026.jpg | nominee1 = '''[[Katie Hobbs]]''' | party1 = Democratic Party (United States) | running_mate1 = '''[[John Giles (American politician)|John Giles]]''' | popular_vote1 = '''1,434,824''' | percentage1 = '''55.63%''' | image2 = Andy Biggs 2025.jpg | nominee2 = [[Andy Biggs]] | party2 = Republican Party (United States) | running_mate2 = [[Sine Kerr]] | popular_vote2 = 1,094,393 | percentage2 = 42.43% | map_image = {{switcher |[[File:2026 Arizona gubernatorial election results map by county.svg|220px]] |County results |[[File:26 Arizona gubernatorial election results map by congressional district.svg|220px]] |Congressional district results }} | map_caption = '''Hobbs:''' {{legend0|#a5b0ff|40-50}} {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674de|60–70%}} {{legend0|#584cde|70–80%}} {{legend0|#3933e5|80-90%}}
'''Biggs:''' {{legend0|#ffb2b2|40–50%}} {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}} {{legend0|#d72f30|70–80%}} | title = [[Governor of Arizona|Governor]] | before_election = [[Katie Hobbs]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Katie Hobbs]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsAZ}} The '''2026 Arizona gubernatorial election''' was held on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Arizona]]. [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] incumbent [[Katie Hobbs]] won a second term, defeating [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] [[United States House of Representatives|congressman]] [[Andy Biggs]].{{Cite web |date=2026-11-04 |title=Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs wins re-election over GOP Rep. Andy Biggs in Arizona |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-election/katie-hobbs-arizona-governor-election-democrat-win-gop-rep-andy-biggs-rcna603354 |access-date=2026-11-06 |website=NBC News |language=en}} Her 13-point margin of victory was a significant improvement over her performance in the [[2022 Arizona gubernatorial election|2022 election]], which she won by 0.67%. [[Primary elections]] took place on July 21, 2026.{{Cite web|date=May 9, 2025 |title=2026 State Primary Election Dates |url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|website= NCSL |access-date=5 August 2025}} Hobbs secured the Democratic nomination unopposed. Biggs secured the Republican nomination over congressman [[David Schweikert]] with 73.6% of the vote.{{Cite web|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-primary-elections/arizona-governor-results|title=Arizona Governor Primary Results|work=[[NBC News]]|access-date=July 22, 2026}} Following the passage of Proposition 131 in the [[2022 Arizona elections|2022 elections]], this was the first gubernatorial election in Arizona in which candidates would be required to nominate a [[running mate]] for the newly established position of [[Lieutenant Governor of Arizona|lieutenant governor]].{{cite news |title=Arizona will elect its first lieutenant governor in 2026. What to know about the role |first=Stacey |last=Barchenger |work=[[The Arizona Republic]] |date=September 21, 2023 |access-date=October 14, 2024 |url=https://www.azcentral.com/story/news/politics/arizona/2023/09/21/arizona-will-elect-its-first-lieutenant-governor-in-2026-what-to-know/70848159007/}} This was one of five Democratic-held governorships up for election in 2026 in a state that [[Donald Trump]] won in the [[2024 United States presidential election|2024 presidential election]]. {{toclimit|3}} == Background == Arizona is considered to be a [[purple state]] at both the federal and statewide level. After [[Joe Biden]] carried the state narrowly in the [[2020 United States presidential election in Arizona|2020 presidential election]],[https://www.cnn.com/2020/11/12/politics/biden-wins-arizona Biden carries Arizona, flipping a longtime Republican stronghold], ''[[CNN]]'', November 13, 2020 [[Donald Trump]] carried the state of Arizona by 5.5 points in the [[2024 United States presidential election in Arizona|2024 presidential election]].[https://news.sky.com/story/us-election-how-big-a-win-was-this-for-donald-trump-13250701 US election: How big a win was this for Donald Trump?], ''[[Sky News]]'', January 20, 2025 Democrats control both [[U.S. Senate]] seats in Arizona[https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2024/11/12/democrat-gallego-wins-arizona-senate-race-defining-republican-majority Democrat Gallego wins Arizona, Republicans hold 53-47 US Senate majority], ''[[Al Jazeera]]'', November 12, 2024[https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/mark-kelly-wins-senate-race-in-arizona Mark Kelly wins Senate race in Arizona], ''[[PBS]]'', November 12, 2022 and hold the governorship, secretary of state office, and attorney general office.[https://apnews.com/article/2022-midterm-elections-arizona-governor-hobbs-ceadb2bf55f1d5ec4760f423f1af0204 Hobbs wins Arizona governor's race, flipping state for Dems], ''[[AP News]]'', November 14, 2022[https://www.multistate.us/insider/2024/11/6/post-election-republicans-add-to-strong-hold-of-state-governments Post-Election: Republicans Add to Strong Hold of State Governments], MultiState.US, November 6, 2024 Meanwhile, Republicans maintain a majority in the [[Arizona Senate]] and [[Arizona House of Representatives]],[https://coppercourier.com/2024/11/20/arizona-legislature-republican-2025/ Republicans maintain total control of the Arizona Legislature. Here's what you need to know.], ''[[The Copper Courier]]'', November 20, 2024 and control 6 of the 9 [[U.S. House of Representatives|House of Representatives seats]] in the state.[https://www.azcentral.com/story/news/politics/elections/2024/11/05/arizona-congressional-races-election-results/75904496007/ Republicans keep 6-3 majority in Arizona's US House delegation], ''[[AZ Central]]'', November 13, 2024 Democrats have characterized this race as key to establishing a Democratic [[Government trifecta|trifecta]] in Arizona for the first time in 60 years.{{Cite web |last=Romo |first=Renee |date= December 12, 2025|title=Democrats hoping for Arizona legislature trifecta |url=https://www.kold.com/2025/12/12/democrats-hoping-arizona-legislature-trifecta/ |access-date= March 2, 2026|website= [[KOLD-TV|KOLD]] |language=en}} ==Democratic primary== ===Candidates=== ==== Nominee ==== *[[Katie Hobbs]], incumbent governor (2023–present){{cite news |last1=Govidarao |first1=Sejal |title=Democratic Arizona Gov. '''Hilton:''' {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}} {{legend0|#d72f30|70–80%}} | title = [[Governor of California|Governor]] | before_election = [[Gavin Newsom]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Xavier Becerra]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsCA}} An election was held in the [[United States|U.S.]] state of [[California]] on November 3, 2026, to elect the next [[governor of California]]. The nominees were [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] former secretary of health and human services [[Xavier Becerra]] and [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] political commentator [[Steve Hilton]]. Democratic incumbent [[Gavin Newsom]] was [[Term limits in the United States|ineligible]] to seek re-election to a third term. Becerra defeated Hilton with over 65% of the vote, the best performance from any California gubernatorial candidate since [[Earl Warren|Earl Warren's]] lopsided victory in [[1946 California gubernatorial election|1946]].{{Cite news |last=Gambino |first=Lauren |date=2026-11-04 |title=Xavier Becerra wins California race for governor with vows to resist Trump’s agenda |url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/03/xavier-becerra-steve-hilton-california-governor |access-date=2026-11-14 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}} Becerra flipped several counties that had not voted Democratic since [[2018 California gubernatorial election|2018]],{{efn|[[Lake County, California|Lake]], [[Merced County, California|Merced]], [[Orange County, California|Orange]], [[San Bernardino County, California|San Bernardino]], and [[San Joaquin County, California|San Joaquin]].}} [[2014 California gubernatorial election|2014]],{{efn|[[Stanislaus County, California|Stanislaus]].}} [[1998 California gubernatorial election|1998]],{{efn|[[Riverside County, California|Riverside]].}} [[1978 California gubernatorial election|1978]],{{efn|[[Butte County, California|Butte]], [[Fresno County, California|Fresno]], and [[Kern County, California|Kern]].}} and [[1958 California gubernatorial election|1958]],{{efn|[[Inyo County, California|Inyo]] and [[Tulare County, California|Tulare]].}} notably flipping the traditionally conservative [[Kern County, California|Kern County]], thereby winning every county in [[Southern California]]. The statewide [[Nonpartisan primary|top-two primary election]] was held on June 2, 2026, with Becerra and Hilton advancing to the general election among the 61 candidates on the ballot.{{cite web|url=https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/statewide-elections/2026-primary/cert-list-candidates.pdf|title=Certified List of Candidates for June 2, 2026, Primary Election|website=[[Secretary of State of California]]|date=March 26, 2026}} Republicans have won neither a gubernatorial nor any other statewide election in California since [[2006 California gubernatorial election|2006]]. ==Candidates== ====Canceled debate==== A debate scheduled for March 24, 2026, hosted by the [[USC Center for the Political Future]], [[KABC-TV]], and [[KMEX-DT]],{{cite web|title=Debate for California Governor Includes CPF and ABC7|url=https://dornsife.usc.edu/center-for-political-future/news/california-governor-debate-2026/|date=March 14, 2026| publisher=[[USC Center for the Political Future]]}} was ultimately canceled hours before it was set to begin.{{cite news|title=University cancels California governor debate after accusations of bias from candidates of color|url=https://apnews.com/article/california-governor-debate-usc-candidates-bias-91539c81a8ecaf8612c0eacd04dc1312|first=Sophie|last=Austin|date=March 26, 2026| publisher=[[Associated Press]]}} Using a formula developed by USC political science professor [[Christian R. Grose]] that combined fundraising and polling data, only six candidates were invited: Republicans Bianco and Hilton, and Democrats Mahan, Porter, Steyer, and Swalwell.{{cite news|title=USC cancels California governor debate after excluding candidates of color|url=https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/usc-cancels-california-gov-debate-22093688.php|first=Anabel|last=Sosa|date=March 26, 2026| publisher=[[SFGate]]}} The selection drew criticism from chairs of the black and Latino caucuses, particularly because no nonwhite candidates qualified and because Mahan's strong fundraising offset weaker polling. '''Marx:''' {{legend0|#FFB2B2|40–50%}} {{legend0|#E27F7F|50–60%}} {{legend0|#D75D5D|60–70%}} {{legend0|#D72F30|70–80%}} | title = [[Governor of Colorado|Governor]] | before_election = [[Jared Polis]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Phil Weiser]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) | percentage1 = '''61.13%''' | percentage2 = 33.21% | popular_vote1 = '''1,639,208''' | popular_vote2 = 890,538 }} {{ElectionsCO}} The '''2026 Colorado gubernatorial election''' was held on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Colorado]]. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[Jared Polis]] is [[Term limits in the United States|ineligible]] to seek re-election to a third consecutive term. [[Primary elections]] took place on June 30, 2026.{{Cite web|date=May 9, 2025 |title=2026 State Primary Election Dates |url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|website= NCSL |access-date=5 August 2025}} Colorado Attorney General [[Phil Weiser]] defeated Republican nominee and Marine Corps veteran [[Victor Marx]].{{Cite web |date=2026-11-01 |title=Colorado Governor Election Live Results 2026 |url=https://apnews.com/projects/elections-2026/colorado-governor-results/ |access-date=2026-11-04 |website=AP News |language=en}}{{Cite web |last=Paul |first=Jesse |date=2026-11-04 |title=Democrat Phil Weiser easily beats Republican Victor Marx to become Colorado’s next governor |url=https://coloradosun.com/2026/11/03/colorado-governor-election-results/ |access-date=2026-11-04 |website=The Colorado Sun |language=en-US}} In the Democratic primary, Colorado Attorney General Weiser defeated U.S. senator [[Michael Bennet]]. Weiser will be the second consecutive Jewish governor after Polis. The [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]] has not won a gubernatorial election in Colorado since [[2002 Colorado gubernatorial election|2002]] nor a statewide office since 2016.{{Cite news |last=Times |first=The New York |date=2017-08-01 |title=Colorado University Regents-At-Large Results: Heidi Ganahl Leads |url=https://www.nytimes.com/elections/2016/results/colorado-university-regents-at-large |access-date=2026-04-24 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} Republican nominee Marx's candidacy was mired in controversy; Marx has made a number of dubious claims and has notably stated he is unsure how many people he has killed.{{Cite web |date=May 27, 2026 |title=Full interview: Colorado Republican gubernatorial candidate Victor Marx |url=https://www.9news.com/video/news/politics/full-interview-colorado-republican-gubernatorial-candidate-victor-marx/73-c7e83d54-e098-41c0-b4fb-15457b261b06 |website=9News |language=en-US |access-date=May 29, 2026}} Leading to the Republican primary, both of Marx's opponents indicated they would refuse to endorse him if he won the nomination.{{Cite web |last=Luning |first=Ernest |date=May 27, 2026 |title=Republicans Kirkmeyer, Bottoms say they won’t back Marx if he wins Colorado’s gubernatorial primary |url=https://www.coloradopolitics.com/2026/05/27/republicans-kirkmeyer-bottoms-say-they-wont-back-marx-if-he-wins-colorados-gubernatorial-primary/ |website=Colorado Politics |language=en-US |access-date=July 21, 2026}} == Democratic primary == === Candidates === To move forward to the primary, candidates had to petition onto the ballot or achieve 30% or more at the [[Colorado Democratic Party]] State Assembly. Michael Bennet was the only candidate to petition onto the primary ballot. All other candidates went through the State Assembly process. [[Phil Weiser]] was the only candidate to achieve 30% or more.{{cite news |work=[[Colorado Democratic Party]] |access-date=March 28, 2026 |url=https://www.coloradodems.org/press/colorado-democratic-party-concludes-2026-state-assembly-announces-results?fbclid=IwY2xjawQ1WJ9leHRuA2FlbQIxMQBicmlkETFGQmVobEtQV1Vubk5hT1M0c3J0YwZhcHBfaWQQMjIyMDM5MTc4ODIwMDg5MgABHq17U9MKJ8KzaqEtc_RpLGbfqCD74CWiN0D8uLv96FJS6y-4SGjmCPvQ-I4j_aem_tWJWw7WdgcoqyIBfcyphrw |title=Colorado Democratic Party Concludes 2026 State Assembly, Announces Results}} Bennet's petition was deemed sufficient on March 24, 2026.{{cite news |work=Colorado Secretary of State |access-date=April 15, 2026 |url=https://www.coloradosos.gov/pubs/elections/vote/primaryPetitionCandidates.html |title=2026 Primary Election Petition Candidates Who Submitted Petition Signatures}} ==== Nominee ==== *[[Phil Weiser]], [[Colorado Attorney General|attorney general of Colorado]] (2019–present){{cite news |last1=Paul |first1=Jesse |title=Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser launches 2026 campaign for governor |url=https://coloradosun.com/2025/01/02/phil-weiser-colorado-governor-2026/ |access-date=January 2, 2025 |work=[[The Colorado Sun]] |date=January 2, 2025}} **Running mate: [[Lesley Dahlkemper]], [[Jefferson County, Colorado#Government and infrastructure|Jefferson County commissioner]]{{cite web|last=Paul|first=Jesse|title=Phil Weiser taps Jefferson County commissioner as running mate in Colorado governor's race|website=The Colorado Sun|date=July 22, 2026|url=https://coloradosun.com/2026/07/22/lesley-dahlhemper-phil-weiser-running-mate/|access-date=July 24, 2026}} ====Eliminated in primary==== *[[Michael Bennet]], [[U.S. senator]] (2009–present){{cite web |last1=Kim |first1=Caitlyn |title=Sen. '''Fazio:''' {{legend0|#E27F7F|50–60%}} {{legend0|#D75D5D|60–70%}} | title = [[Governor of Connecticut|Governor]] | before_election = [[Ned Lamont]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Ned Lamont]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }}{{For|related races|2026 United States gubernatorial elections}} {{Elections in Connecticut}} The '''2026 Connecticut gubernatorial election''' took place on November 3, 2026 to elect the [[governor of Connecticut]]. Primary elections took place on August 11, 2026. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[Ned Lamont]] won re-election a third term, defeating Republican nominee and state Senator [[Ryan Fazio]].{{Cite web |last=Glatz |first=Jennifer |date=2026-11-03 |title=Gov. Ned Lamont wins third term as Connecticut's governor. See how your town voted |url=https://www.nbcconnecticut.com/elections/connecticut-governor-election-results-lamont-fazio-midterms/3787870/ |access-date=2026-11-14 |website=NBC Connecticut |language=en-US}}{{Cite news |last=Vigdor |first=Neil |date=2026-08-12 |title=Ned Lamont Wins the Democratic Primary for Connecticut Governor |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/11/us/politics/connecticut-primary-governor-lamont-elliott.html |access-date=2026-08-12 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} This was the best performance for a Democratic gubernatorial candidate since [[1958 Connecticut gubernatorial election|1958]]. Lamont became the first Democrat to win three terms since [[Wilbur Lucius Cross]] in [[1934 Connecticut gubernatorial election|1934]]. Lamont had been one of the most popular governors in the United States, with a 63% approval rating as of October 2026, according to [[Morning Consult]];{{Cite web |title=U.S. Governor Approval Rating Tracker |url=https://pro.morningconsult.com/trackers/governor-approval-ratings |access-date=2025-11-15 |website=Morning Consult Pro |language=en}} however, a [[University of New Hampshire]] poll from May 2025 found that 44% of Connecticut voters believe he should not run for a third term.{{Cite web |last=Craven |first=John |date=June 5, 2025 |title=Gov. Lamont 'seriously' considering running for a rare third term |url=https://connecticut.news12.com/gov-lamont-seriously-considering-running-for-a-rare-third-term |website=News 12 Connecticut}} [[Connecticut House of Representatives|State representative]] [[Josh Elliott (politician)|Josh Elliott]] challenged Lamont in the primary as a [[Progressivism in the United States|progressive]].{{Cite news |last=Putterman |first=Alex |title=State Rep. Josh Elliott announces campaign for governor, promising to tax CT's wealthy |url=https://www.ctinsider.com/politics/article/ct-josh-elliott-governor-lamont-primary-challenge-20768829.php |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260206022833/https://www.ctinsider.com/politics/article/ct-josh-elliott-governor-lamont-primary-challenge-20768829.php |archive-date=2026-02-06 |url-status=live |access-date=2026-02-06 |work=CT Insider |language=en}} {{toclimit|4}} ==Democratic primary== While incumbent [[List of governors of Connecticut|governor]] [[Ned Lamont]] initially had expressed doubts about running for a third term,{{Cite news |last=Haar |first=Dan |title=Dan Haar: Will he run? Lamont interview reveals doubts about a third term for Connecticut governor |url=https://www.ctinsider.com/politics/article/ct-gov-ned-lamont-third-term-20243961.php |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250701001417/https://www.ctinsider.com/politics/article/ct-gov-ned-lamont-third-term-20243961.php |archive-date=2025-07-01 |url-status=live |access-date=2025-11-15 |work=CT Insider |language=en}} he announced that he would run for re-election in November 2025.{{Cite web |last=Pazniokas |first=Mark |date=2025-11-14 |title=Today, the curtain goes up on Ned Lamont's bid for a third term |url=https://ctmirror.org/2025/11/14/gov-lamont-reelection-third-term-announcement/ |access-date=2025-11-15 |website=CT Mirror |language=en-US}} [[Connecticut House of Representatives|State representative]] [[Josh Elliott (politician)|Josh Elliott]] had already launched a bid to primary Lamont, believing that Connecticut needed a more [[Progressivism in the United States|progressive]] leader.{{Cite news |last=Craven |first=John |date=2025-07-14 |title=Democrat Josh Elliott launches bid for governor, promising big shift from Lamont |url=https://connecticut.news12.com/2025/07/14/democrat-josh-elliott-launches-bid-for-governor-promising-big-shift-from/4fXhwKnBB4lof6pdqcoKJs |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260518211332/https://connecticut.news12.com/2025/07/14/democrat-josh-elliott-launches-bid-for-governor-promising-big-shift-from/4fXhwKnBB4lof6pdqcoKJs |archive-date=2026-05-18 |access-date=2026-05-18 |work=News 12 Connecticut}} At the Democratic State Convention on May 16, 2026, at [[The Bushnell Center for the Performing Arts|The Bushnell]] in [[Hartford, Connecticut|Hartford]], Lamont defeated Elliott for the [[Democratic Party of Connecticut|state party]] endorsement, 1,468 votes (74.6%) to 501 (25.4%). However, Elliott surpassed the 15% of delegates needed to get on the ballot for the primary, which took place on August 11;{{Cite web |last=Brown |first=Andrew |date=2026-05-16 |title=CT Dems endorse Lamont for 3rd term, but he faces primary |url=https://ctmirror.org/2026/05/16/lamont-clinches-ct-democratic-party-endorsement-but-will-face-primary/ |access-date=2026-05-18 |website=CT Mirror |language=en-US}} Lamont was the first incumbent governor to face a primary since [[Ella Grasso]] in [[1978 Connecticut gubernatorial election|1978]]. Lamont would go on to win the primary, and the party's endorsement. ===Governor=== ====Candidates==== =====Nominee===== *[[Ned Lamont]], incumbent governor (2019–present){{cite news |author=Mike Cerulli |title=Ned Lamont to run for third term as Connecticut governor in 2026 |url=https://www.wtnh.com/news/elections/ned-lamont-to-run-for-third-term-as-connecticut-governor-in-2026-sources/ |work=[[WTNH]] |date=November 7, 2025}} =====Eliminated in primary===== *[[Josh Elliott (politician)|Josh Elliott]], [[Connecticut House of Representatives|state representative]] from [[Connecticut's 88th House of Representatives district|HD-88]] (2017–present){{cite news |work=CT Insider |access-date=July 14, 2025 |url=https://www.ctinsider.com/politics/article/ct-josh-elliott-governor-lamont-primary-challenge-20768829.php |author=Putterman, Alex |date=July 14, 2025 |title=State Rep. [[Betsy McCaughey]] received about 8% of the vote, falling well short of the 15% threshold needed to force an August primary, and quickly endorsed Fazio.{{Cite web |last=Pazniokas |first=Mark |date=2026-05-16 |title=Ryan Fazio wins the CT GOP nomination for governor |url=https://ctmirror.org/2026/05/16/ryan-fazio-wins-the-ct-gop-nomination-for-governor/ |access-date=2026-05-17 |website=CT Mirror |language=en-US}} In the following months before the convention, [[Erin Stewart]], the former mayor of [[New Britain, Connecticut|New Britain]], was seen as the frontrunner in a tight race with Fazio. '''Jolly:''' {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674de|60–70%}} {{legend0|#584cde|70–80%}} | title = [[Governor of Florida|Governor]] | before_election = [[Ron DeSantis]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Byron Donalds]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{Elections in Florida sidebar}} The 2026 Florida gubernatorial election took place in the US state on November 3, 2026, to elect the governor of Florida. Republican Representative [[Byron Donalds]] narrowly defeated former Representative [[David Jolly]]. Incumbent two-term Republican governor [[Ron DeSantis]] was term-limited and ineligible for a third term. Primary elections were held on August 18, 2026. In the Republican primary, Representative Byron Donalds won with 47.8% of the vote. In the Democratic primary, former Representative [[David Jolly]] won with 61.0% of the vote. The election ended up being closely contested, highlighting a stronger-than-expected Democratic challenge in a state that had increasingly favored Republicans. Donalds' victory was historic as Florida’s first African American governor and the first elected African American Republican governor in U.S. history. The narrow Republican victory also marked a significant contrast with the party's landslide gubernatorial win in [[2022 Florida gubernatorial election|2022]]. This was the second consecutive Florida gubernatorial election in which the Democratic nominee was a former Republican and the eighth consecutive victory for Republicans.{{Cite news |last=Welch |first=Catherine |date=2026-11-03 |title=Republican Byron Donalds wins governor's race in Florida |url=https://www.npr.org/2026/11/03/g-s1-151260/florida-governor-donalds-jolly |access-date=2026-11-14 |work=NPR |language=en}} == Background == A heavily populated [[South Atlantic states|South Atlantic state]] with a large and increasingly conservative [[Hispanic and Latino Americans|Latino American]] population and the northern parts lying in the [[Bible Belt]], Florida is considered to be a moderately to strongly [[red states and blue states|red state]], having not elected a Democratic governor since [[1994 Florida gubernatorial election|1994]] nor a Democrat for president since [[2012 United States presidential election|2012]] and having moved significantly rightward in the last decade.{{cite web |last1=Mazzei |first1=Patricia |date=October 29, 2024 |title=Florida Stopped Being a Swing State Slowly, Then All at Once |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/10/29/us/florida-trump-republicans-swing-state.html |access-date=March 7, 2026 |website=The New York Times}} In [[2022 Florida gubernatorial election|2022]], incumbent governor [[Ron DeSantis]] was re-elected by a 19.4% margin, a considerable improvement from his 0.4-point victory four years earlier in the [[2018 Florida gubernatorial election|gubernatorial election]] during the [[2018 blue wave]]. This was followed in 2024 by Republican [[Donald Trump]] winning his adoptive home state by a 13% margin as he won a second non-consecutive presidential term, improving his 3.4% margin of victory in [[2020 United States presidential election in Florida|2020]] and seemingly diminishing Florida's longtime [[swing state|swing-state]] and [[Florida bellwether|bellwether]] status. Republicans also control all statewide offices, a large majority of the state's U.S. House delegation, both U.S. Senate seats, and supermajorities in both houses of the [[Florida Legislature]].{{cite web |title=Party control of Florida state government |url=https://ballotpedia.org/Party_control_of_Florida_state_government |access-date=March 7, 2026 |website=Ballotpedia |language=en}} === Candidate eligibility and requirements === Article IV, Section 5(b) of the [[Constitution of Florida|Florida Constitution]] states that, for a person to serve as governor, they must:{{Cite web |title=Article IV, Florida Constitution |url=https://ballotpedia.org/Article_IV,_Florida_Constitution |access-date=May 13, 2023 |website=[[Ballotpedia]]}} * Be at least thirty years old; * Be a permanent resident of Florida for at least seven years; * Not have served as governor for six years or more of the two prior terms. == Republican primary == [[File:Official portrait of Lieutenant Governor of Florida Jay Collins (cropped 5).jpg|thumb|x170px|[[Lieutenant Governor of Florida]] [[Jay Collins]] finished second in the primary.]] === Candidates === ==== Nominee ==== * [[Byron Donalds]], [[U.S. representative]] for {{ushr|FL|19}} (2021–present){{cite news |last1=Leonard |first1=Kimberly |last2=Matat |first2=Stephany |date=February 25, 2025 |title=Rep. The party stated that they had made the decision to cancel the debate after no candidate except Donalds met its qualifications. The party's minimum requirements for a candidate to participate included: * At least 10% support in a Republican party-sponsored primary voter poll * A minimum $10 million in raised contributions * Over 10,000 unique individual campaign donors The announcement drew criticism from gubernatorial candidates Collins, Fishback, and Renner, as well as incumbent Governor [[Ron DeSantis]]. DeSantis attacked the party for trying to "engineer the outcome" of the primary election and acting against "the best interest of Republican voters." DeSantis additionally noted that he himself would not have qualified under the set criteria during his [[Ron DeSantis#2018 candidacy|2018 primary run]].{{cite news |last=Ellenbogen |first=Romy |date=June 12, 2026 |title=DeSantis hits Florida GOP over Republican primary debate |url=https://www.tampabay.com/news/florida-politics/elections/2026/06/12/florida-desantis-gop-republican-debate-donalds-fishback/ |work=Tampa Bay Times}} The ''[[Miami Herald]]'' also panned the decision, calling for a primary debate to take place.{{cite news |author=Miami-Herald Editorial Board |date=June 23, 2026 |title=Florida GOP canceled the debate, but the real story is why they did it - Opinion |url=https://www.miamiherald.com/opinion/editorials/article316224360.html |work=[[Miami Herald]]}} On June 24, [[WJAX-TV]] announced that the planned CBS debate would be cancelled, after "a majority of the Republican candidates didn’t agree to participate." Only Fishback and Renner agreed to debate, with Collins stating that he would only accept if Donalds showed as well. Donalds refused to participate in any debate, leading Fishback labeling Donalds a "coward".{{cite news |last=Stofan |first=Jake |date=June 24, 2026 |title=With 2 candidates refusing to commit, Action News Jax will not host GOP Gubernatorial Primary debate |url=https://www.actionnewsjax.com/news/local/with-2-candidates-refusing-commit-action-news-jax-will-not-host-gop-gubernatorial-primary-debate/3FI5T5XLNBGGRJ2YQHC5IX6TWI/ |work=Action News Jax}} On June 25, Renner announced on X that the planned Fox 13 debate, set for July 21, had been cancelled.{{cite tweet |number=2070193010164318251 |user=Paul_Renner |title=I just learned that the proposed Fox 13 debate in Tampa on July 21st has been canceled. [[Keisha Lance Bottoms]], a [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrat]] and former [[Mayor of Atlanta|Atlanta Mayor]], defeated [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] billionaire businessman [[Rick Jackson (businessman)|Rick Jackson]].{{cite web|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-elections/georgia-governor-results|title=Georgia Governor Results 2026|publisher=[[NBC News]]|access-date=November 3, 2026}} [[Primary elections]] were held on May 19, 2026, with a primary runoff held on June 16. Jackson and incumbent Lieutenant Governor [[Burt Jones]] received the most votes in the first round of the Republican primary, but failed to reach the 50% threshold, causing a runoff which Jackson won. Jackson's campaign was predominantly self-funded, managing to overcome endorsements for Jones from President [[Donald Trump]] and outgoing governor [[Brian Kemp]]. Bottoms won the Democratic nomination without a runoff against six other candidates. This race was expected to be highly competitive due to the state's nearly even partisan lean and Bottoms' perceived poor electability. Most polling showed the two candidates within the margin of error. However, in the midst of a [[2026 United States elections|historic Democratic wave]] nationwide, Keisha Lance Bottoms unexpectedly pulled away on election night and won by a comfortable 8.6% margin, the largest for a Democrat since [[1986 Georgia gubernatorial election|1986]] and much to her own surprise.{{Cite web |date=2026-11-04 |title=Keisha Lance Bottoms surprised by lopsided win in Georgia governor's race: "I thought it could be much closer" - CBS News |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/keisha-lance-bottoms-georgia-governor/ |access-date=2026-11-07 |website=www.cbsnews.com |language=en-US}} Along with her victory, Democrats won every other statewide office in Georgia on the [[2026 Georgia state elections|same ballot]].{{Cite web |title=Georgia Democrats flip every statewide office, but appear to fall short in the Senate {{!}} |url=https://capitol-beat.org/2026/11/georgia-democrats-flip-every-statewide-office-but-appear-to-fall-short-in-the-senate/ |access-date=2026-11-06 |website=capitol-beat.org}} Bottoms is the first woman and first African-American to be elected governor of Georgia. Bottoms will be the first African-American woman to be governor of any U.S. state. She is the first Democrat to be elected governor of Georgia since [[Roy Barnes]] in [[1998 Georgia gubernatorial election|1998]].{{cite news |title=Keisha Lance Bottoms wins Georgia governor race; Jackson concedes |url=https://www.fox5atlanta.com/news/bottoms-wins-georgia-governor-race-after-jackson-concedes |access-date=November 4, 2026 |publisher=Fox 5 Atlanta |date=November 3, 2026}} == Republican primary == === Candidates === Incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] governor [[Brian Kemp]] was [[Term limits in the United States|ineligible]] to seek re-election to a third consecutive term. With Kemp term-limited, speculation mounted about Lieutenant Governor [[Burt Jones]], Secretary of State [[Brad Raffensperger]], and Attorney General [[Chris Carr (politician)|Chris Carr]]. Carr and Raffensperger sought to associate themselves with Kemp, drawing on his relative popularity.{{cite news |last1=Timotija |first1=Filip |title=Georgia attorney general launches bid in 2026 governor's race |url=https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/5003295-georgia-chris-carr-governor-race/ |access-date=October 7, 2026 |date=November 21, 2024}} Jones sought to ally himself with Trump, who endorsed him in August 2025. Rick Jackson, a healthcare CEO, announced his campaign in February 2026. Previously unknown in the political realm, Jackson quickly consolidated support from right-wing primary voters, in part due to his significant personal financial resources. Jackson spent more than $83 million in personal funds during the primary. Jackson's campaign emphasized his success as a self-made billionaire, highlighting his impoverished childhood. Jackson also sought to tie himself to Trump, claiming he would be "Trump's favorite governor" and "just like Trump, but with a Southern tone."{{cite news |title=Burt Jones was the inevitable Republican nominee for Georgia governor. Then Rick Jackson showed up |url=https://apnews.com/article/rick-jackson-georgia-governor-burt-jones-trump-4c1789c599857e220180068e26de9199 |access-date=October 7, 2026 |work=AP News |date=March 14, 2026}} An aggressive television ad campaign allowed Jackson to take a small polling lead by spring 2026. Jackson's self-funding represented the largest amount any candidate had ever spent in a primary race for Georgia governor. Jones's campaign focused primarily on rural connections, Trump, and support from Republican allies in the General Assembly. Jones accused Jackson of "[making] his fortune recruiting for [[Planned Parenthood]]" and funding [[Transgender surgery]] for minors.{{cite news |last1=Bynum |first1=Zachary |title=Georgia GOP With the Democratic primary already over, focus shifted to the candidates' ability to counter Keisha Lance Bottoms. However, the state maintained a Republican lean at the state level, with Republicans holding all statewide executive offices in the [[2022 Georgia elections|2022 midterms]], where incumbent governor Brian Kemp was [[2022 Georgia gubernatorial election|re-elected]] in a rematch against [[Democratic Party of Georgia|Democrat]] [[Stacey Abrams]] by a 7.5 percent margin.{{Cite news |last=Bluestein |first=Greg |title=Abrams says she will 'likely run again.' That doesn't excite some Democrats |language=English |work=[[The Atlanta Journal-Constitution]] |url=https://www.ajc.com/politics/abrams-says-she-will-likely-run-again-that-doesnt-excite-some-democrats/23WS3YRCB5E5FEVI5DPK6PU6LA/ |access-date=2023-05-13 |issn=1539-7459 |date=March 16, 2023}} Republicans also control both the [[Georgia State Senate|state senate]] and [[Georgia House of Representatives|House of Representatives]], together with Kemp's governorship establishing a [[government trifecta]], alongside an all but one Republican pick on the [[Supreme Court of Georgia (U.S. state)|state's supreme court]]. A year prior to the 2026 elections, the [[2025 Georgia Public Service Commission special election|2025 Georgia Public Service Commission (PSC) special election]] resulted in two Democrats being elected to the Commission, both by landslide victories, and marking the first time that Democrats won any seats on the PSC since the [[2000 Georgia state elections|2000 elections]] or any state-wide non-federal offices since the [[2006 Georgia state elections|2006 elections]].{{Cite web |last=Vakil |first=Caroline |date=November 4, 2025 |title=Democrats win key Georgia special elections seen as midterm bellwethers |url=https://thehill.com/homenews/5589670-gop-incumbents-lose-seats/ |access-date=November 12, 2025 |website=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]]}}{{Cite web |last=Jones |first=Emily |date=2025-11-06 |title=What Georgia Democrats' PSC wins could mean for power bills and the midterm elections |url=https://www.wabe.org/what-democrats-psc-wins-could-mean-for-power-bills-and-the-midterm-elections/ |access-date=2025-11-12 |website=WABE |language=en-US}} Democrats had not won a gubernatorial election in Georgia since [[1998 Georgia gubernatorial election|1998]].{{cn|date=November 2026}} Bottoms became the first gubernatorial Democratic candidate to win [[Houston County, GA|Houston County]] (home to [[Warner Robins]]) since [[Roy Barnes]] in 1998; '''Lahn:''' {{legend0|#FFB2B2|40–50%}} {{legend0|#E27F7F|50–60%}} {{legend0|#D75D5D|60–70%}} {{legend0|#D72F30|70–80%}} {{legend0|#c21b18|80–90%}} {{legend0|#A80000|>90%}} | title = [[Governor of Iowa|Governor]] | before_election = [[Kim Reynolds]] | before_party = Republican Party of Iowa | after_election = [[Rob Sand]] | after_party = [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] }} {{ElectionsIA}} The '''2026 Iowa gubernatorial election''' was held on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Iowa]]. [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] state auditor [[Rob Sand]] won the election against [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] businessman Zach Lahn.{{Cite web |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/us/iowa-governor-sand-lahn.html |last=Bosman |first=Julie |title=Rob Sand Is Elected Iowa Governor, Ending Republicans' Hold on the Seat |date=November 3, 2026 |access-date=November 4, 2026 |website=[[The New York Times]]}} Republican incumbent [[Kim Reynolds]] did not seek a third full term. [[Primary elections]] were held on June 2, 2026.{{Cite web|date=January 1, 2025|title=State of Iowa Election Calendar 2026|url=https://sos.iowa.gov/elections/pdf/cal3yr.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260521023253/https://sos.iowa.gov/elections/pdf/cal3yr.pdf|archive-date=May 21, 2026|access-date=April 18, 2025|publisher=[[Secretary of State of Iowa]]}} In the Republican primary, Representative [[Randy Feenstra]] emerged as the frontrunner after being endorsed by President [[Donald Trump]], but Lahn won the nomination in an [[Upset (competition)|upset]] with 37.65% of the vote. Sand was the only candidate to qualify for the ballot in the Democratic primary. Leading up to the election, Rob Sand was the only Democrat holding statewide elected office in Iowa, as the state has trended reliably red in recent years. With the incumbent's retirement and Sand's entry, pollsters considered the governor's mansion a potential offensive opportunity for Democrats. Aided by his personal popularity, questions about his opponent's residency, as well as a national environment that was expected to favor his party, Sand led his opponent in the vast majority of pre-election polling, oftentimes outside the margin of error. Come election night, Rob Sand won, defeating Zach Lahn by an 11% margin. This was the first open gubernatorial election in Iowa since [[2006 Iowa gubernatorial election|2006]] and the first time since that election that Democrats won the governorship.{{cite news |title=Democrat Rob Sand wins Iowa governor's race, ending GOP control of the office |url=https://www.houstonpublicmedia.org/npr/2026/11/04/g-s1-151136/democrat-rob-sand-wins-iowa-governors-race-ending-gop-control-of-the-office/ |access-date=November 4, 2026 |publisher=Houston Public Media |date=November 4, 2026}} Sand won by the largest margin for a Democratic Iowa gubernatorial candidate since [[1964 Iowa gubernatorial election|1964]]. == Background == [[Iowa]] is considered to be a moderate-to-strong [[Red states and blue states|red state]], with both chambers of its state legislature controlled by the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]]. However, in [[2025 Iowa elections#State legislative|special elections in 2025]], Iowa Republicans lost their supermajority in the [[Iowa Senate]].{{cite news |title=Democrat Renee Hardman wins Iowa state Senate seat, blocking GOP from reclaiming supermajority |url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/amp/politics/democrat-renee-hardman-wins-iowa-state-senate-seat-blocking-gop-from-reclaiming-supermajority |access-date=October 7, 2026 |publisher=PBS |date=December 31, 2025}} Republicans still maintain their supermajority in the [[Iowa House of Representatives]] that they won in [[2024 Iowa House of Representatives election|2024]].{{cite news |title=GOP at risk of significant state legislative losses, Post analysis finds |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/10/06/its-not-just-congress-how-midterms-can-reshape-state-by-state-power/ |access-date=October 7, 2026 |publisher=Washington Post |date=October 6, 2026}} The last time the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic Party]] won a gubernatorial election in Iowa was in [[2006 Iowa gubernatorial election|2006]]. All four members of the [[United States House of Representatives|U.S. House of Representatives]] from Iowa have been Republicans since [[2022 United States House of Representatives elections in Iowa|2022]] and Republicans had won all [[United States Senate|U.S. Senate]] elections in Iowa since 2010, making Iowa's congressional delegation entirely Republican. In Presidential Elections, Iowa voted for Republican President [[Donald Trump]] in his nationwide-win in [[2016 United States presidential election in Iowa|2016]], loss in [[2020 United States presidential election in Iowa|2020]], and win again in [[2024 United States presidential election in Iowa|2024]], with Trump's and the Republican Party's vote-share increasing in Iowa in every subsequent election.{{Cite web |last=McCue |first=Dan |title=Des Moines Register Poll Reconfirms Iowa’s Shift From Swing to Red State
