Though originally from Iowa, Zach Lahn faced scrutiny following reporting by ''[[The Des Moines Register]]'' that he lived in [[Kansas]] until 2023, when he allegedly returned to Iowa.{{Cite news |last=Henderson |first=O. Kay |date=June 5, 2026 |title=Sand suggests Lahn should have run for governor in another state - Radio Iowa |url=https://www.radioiowa.com/2026/06/05/sand-suggests-lahn-should-have-run-for-governor-in-another-state/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260607080158/https://www.radioiowa.com/2026/06/05/sand-suggests-lahn-should-have-run-for-governor-in-another-state/ |archive-date=June 7, 2026 |access-date=July 2, 2026 |work=Radio Iowa |language=en-US |url-status=live}} Lahn registered to vote in [[Iowa]] on October 17, 2024, ahead of the 2024 election.{{Cite web |last=Carpenter |first=Tim |date=May 29, 2026 |title=Co-founder of Wichita private school contending for Iowa GOP's gubernatorial nomination • Kansas Reflector |url=https://kansasreflector.com/2026/05/29/co-founder-of-wichita-private-school-contending-for-iowa-gops-gubernatorial-nomination/ |access-date=July 7, 2026 |website=Kansas Reflector |language=en-US}} The newspaper later reported that flight records indicated Lahn spent 75 nights in [[Wichita, Kansas]], between October 2025 and spring 2026, frequently traveling there by private plane.{{Cite web |last=Larson |first=Luke |date=June 19, 2026 |title=Lahn defends Iowa residency amid campaign criticism |url=https://who13.com/news/politics/iowa-politics/lahn-defends-iowa-residency-amid-campaign-criticism/ |website=WHO13 Des Moines}} Lahn said the trips were related to custody arrangements involving his children, who live in Kansas. {{short description|none}} {{for|related races|2026 United States gubernatorial elections}} {{Use American English|date=January 2025}} {{Use mdy dates|date=November 2026}} {{Infobox election | election_name = 2026 Illinois gubernatorial election | country = Illinois | type = presidential | last_update = 9:46 AM | time_zone = [[Central Standard Time|CST]] | previous_election = 2022 Illinois gubernatorial election | previous_year = 2022 | next_election = 2030 Illinois gubernatorial election | next_year = 2030 | election_date = November 3, 2026 | image1 = JB Pritzker 2026 (cropped 3x4).jpg | nominee1 = '''[[JB Pritzker]]''' | party1 = Democratic Party (United States) | running_mate1 = '''[[Christian Mitchell]]''' | popular_vote1 = '''2,575,452''' | percentage1 = '''60.82%''' | image2 = Darren Bailey at a 2022 Campaign Event (cropped2).jpg | nominee2 = [[Darren Bailey]] | party2 = Republican Party (United States) | running_mate2 = Aaron Del Mar | popular_vote2 = 1,516,799 | percentage2 = 35.82% | map_image = {{switcher |[[File:2026 Illinois gubernatorial election results map by county.svg|160px]] |County results}} | map_caption = '''Pritzker:''' {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674de|60–70%}} {{legend0|#584cde|70–80%}}
'''Bailey:''' {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}} {{legend0|#d72f30|70–80%}} {{legend0|#c21b18|80–90%}} | title = [[Governor of Illinois|Governor]] | before_election = [[JB Pritzker]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[JB Pritzker]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsIL}} The '''2026 Illinois gubernatorial election''' was held on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Illinois]]. [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] incumbent [[JB Pritzker]] sought a third term in office against [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] nominee [[Darren Bailey]], whom he defeated in [[2022 Illinois gubernatorial election|2022]]. Pritzker defeated Bailey a second time, becoming the first Illinois governor to be reelected to a third term since [[Jim Thompson (Illinois politician)|Jim Thompson]] in [[1982 Illinois gubernatorial election|1982]], and the first Democrat to do so in the state's history.{{Cite web |last=Sharkey |first=Dylan |date=November 4, 2026 |title=Pritzker first Democrat to win 3 terms as Illinois governor |url=https://www.illinoispolicy.org/pritzker-first-democrat-to-win-3-terms-as-illinois-governor/ |access-date=November 6, 2026 |website=Illinois Policy}}{{Cite web |last=Moreland |first=Brianna |date=June 27, 2025 |title=Governor Pritzker aims for historic third term, first since Jim Thompson's tenure |url=https://abc3340.com/news/nation-world/governor-pritzker-aims-for-historic-third-term-first-since-jim-thompsons-tenure |access-date=November 7, 2026 |website=WBMA |language=en}} Pritzker outperformed his 2022 margin of victory by double digits. [[Primary elections]] were held on March 17, 2026.{{Cite web |last=Illinois State Board of Elections |title=Schedule of Future Elections |url=https://www.elections.il.gov/agencyforms/1%20SCHEDULE%20OF%20FUTURE%20ELECTIONS/Schedule%20of%20Elections%20-%20Revised.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260221135507/https://www.elections.il.gov/agencyforms/1%20SCHEDULE%20OF%20FUTURE%20ELECTIONS/Schedule%20of%20Elections%20-%20Revised.pdf |archive-date=February 21, 2026 |access-date=July 21, 2025 |website=www.elections.il.gov}} Pritzker secured the Democratic nomination unopposed, while [[Darren Bailey]] secured the Republican nomination with 54% of the vote.{{cite web |title=Illinois Governor Primary Results 2026 |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-primary-elections/illinois-governor-results |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260411230100/https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-primary-elections/illinois-governor-results |archive-date=April 11, 2026 |access-date=April 19, 2026 |website=[[NBC News]]}} Pritzker selected [[Christian Mitchell]] as his running mate, as incumbent lieutenant governor [[Juliana Stratton]] ran as the Democratic nominee for [[2026 United States Senate election in Illinois|U.S. Senate]]. The election was the first gubernatorial rematch in Illinois since [[1986 Illinois gubernatorial election|1986]]. In the general election, Pritzker won with over 60% of the vote, an improvement of over five percentage points from 2022. This is the first time a Democratic candidate for governor has won 60% or more of the vote in Illinois, as well as the first time [[Sangamon County, Illinois|Sangamon County]] went for the Democratic candidate for governor since [[1964 Illinois gubernatorial election|1964]],{{Cite news |last=Szalinski |first=Ben |last2=Moore |first2=Brenden |date=November 4, 2026 |title=Pritzker wins third term as IL governor. Will he run for president? |url=https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/pritzker-wins-third-term-as-il-governor-will-he-run-for-president/ar-AA2gL26Z |access-date=November 6, 2026 |work=Belleville News-Democrat |publisher=MSN|at=para. 30}} and the first time for [[McHenry County, Illinois|McHenry County]] since [[1852 Illinois gubernatorial election|1852]].{{Cite web |last=Schmidt|first=Rose |date=November 5, 2026 |title=Illinois county votes for Democratic gubernatorial candidate for first time since 1852 |url=https://www.nbcchicago.com/news/local/illinois-county-votes-for-democratic-gubernatorial-candidate-for-first-time-since-1852/4013088/ |access-date=November 8, 2026 |website=NBC Chicago |language=en-US}} == Background == A moderately to strongly Democratic state, Illinois has a reputation for being both the most populous and the most left-leaning state in the Midwest, largely due to the progressive and diverse [[Chicago metropolitan area]]. While the state favored Republicans for [[Governor of Illinois|governor]] during the 1970s to 1990s, Democrats have won all but one gubernatorial race in Illinois since [[2002 Illinois gubernatorial election|2002]], the exception being [[Bruce Rauner]]'s narrow victory in [[2014 Illinois gubernatorial election|2014]].{{Cite web |last=Leip |first=David |title=2014 Gubernatorial General Election Results – Illinois |url=https://uselectionatlas.org/RESULTS/state.php?year=2014&fips=17&f=0&off=5&elect=0 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250404104935/https://uselectionatlas.org/RESULTS/state.php?fips=17&year=2014&f=0&off=5&elect=0 |archive-date=April 4, 2025 |access-date=April 9, 2025 |website=uselectionatlas.org}} In addition, Democrats have occupied all of its statewide offices since [[2018 Illinois elections|2019]] and have won by double-digit margins in every presidential election since [[1992 United States presidential election in Illinois|1992]]. Incumbent governor [[JB Pritzker]], a member of the Democratic Party, comfortably won the previous two elections, having first been elected with a 15.6% lead in [[2018 Illinois gubernatorial election|2018]]{{Cite web |last=Leip |first=David |title=2018 Gubernatorial General Election Results – Illinois |url=https://uselectionatlas.org/results/state.php?year=2018&fips=17&f=0&off=5&elect=0 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240520050528/https://uselectionatlas.org/RESULTS/state.php?fips=17&year=2018&f=0&off=5&elect=0 |archive-date=May 20, 2024 |access-date=April 9, 2025 |website=uselectionatlas.org}} and won re-election by 12.5% in [[2022 Illinois gubernatorial election|2022]].{{Cite web |last=Leip |first=David |title=2022 Gubernatorial General Election Results – Illinois |url=https://uselectionatlas.org/results/state.php?year=2022&fips=17&f=0&off=5&elect=0 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240419033643/https://uselectionatlas.org/RESULTS/state.php?fips=17&year=2022&f=0&off=5&elect=0 |archive-date=April 19, 2024 |access-date=April 9, 2025 |website=uselectionatlas.org}} Despite the state's strong Democratic lean, Republicans are comfortably favored in most of rural Illinois, especially in much of [[Forgottonia|West Central]] and [[Southern Illinois]]. 2026 Kansas gubernatorial election.text:
{{short description|none}} {{for|related races|2026 United States gubernatorial elections}} {{Use American English|date=January 2025}} {{Use mdy dates|date=November 2026}} {{Infobox election | election_name = 2026 Kansas gubernatorial election | country = Kansas | type = presidential | last_update = November 12, 2:45 PM | time_zone = [[Central Standard Time|CST]]{{Cite web |url=https://civicapi.org/decision-2026 |title=America's Decision 2026 |website=CivicAPI |access-date=November 4, 2026}} | previous_election = 2022 Kansas gubernatorial election | previous_year = 2022 | next_election = 2030 Kansas gubernatorial election | next_year = 2030 | election_date = November 3, 2026 | image1 = Cindy Holscher 1 (3x4 cropped).jpg | nominee1 = '''[[Cindy Holscher]]''' | party1 = Democratic Party (United States) | running_mate1 = '''[[KC Ohaebosim]]''' | popular_vote1 = '''562,012''' | percentage1 = '''50.51%''' | image2 = 3x4.svg | image_size = 150x150px | nominee2 = [[Ty Masterson]] | party2 = Republican Party (United States) | running_mate2 = [[Jeff Klemp]] | popular_vote2 = 550,643 | percentage2 = 49.49% | map_image = {{switcher |[[File:2026 Kansas gubernatorial election results map by county.svg|270px]] |County results |[[File:2022 Kansas attorney general election results map by congressional district.svg|270px]] |Congressional district results}} | map_caption = '''Holscher:''' {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674de|60–70%}} {{legend0|#584cde|70–80%}}
'''Masterson:''' {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}} {{legend0|#d72f30|70–80%}} {{legend0|#C21B18|80–90%}} | title = [[Governor of Kansas|Governor]] | before_election = [[Laura Kelly]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Cindy Holscher]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) | turnout = }} {{ElectionsKS}} The '''2026 Kansas gubernatorial election''' took place on November 3, 2026, to elect the next [[List of governors of Kansas|governor of Kansas]]. The primary elections took place on August 4, 2026.{{Cite web|date=May 9, 2025 |title=2026 State Primary Election Dates |url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|publisher=NCSL |access-date=August 5, 2025}} Democrat [[Cindy Holscher]] was declared the winner on November 12, 2026, over Republican [[Ty Masterson]].{{Cite news |last=Hanna |first=John |date=November 12, 2026 |title=Democrat Cindy Holscher is elected Kansas' next governor, extending her party's wave of victories |url=https://apnews.com/article/kansas-governor-midterm-election-cindy-holscher-c9bb46dfd593fa7182a6bc93722ce552 |access-date=November 12, 2026 |work=[[Associated Press]]}} Holscher's victory was the first time a party won the governorship for the third consecutive time since [[1970 Kansas gubernatorial election|1970]] when Democratic governor [[Robert Docking]] won his third of four two-year terms. Holscher was the first Kansas gubernatorial candidate to receive over 50% of the vote since Republican [[Sam Brownback]] in [[2010 Kansas gubernatorial election|2010]], and the first Democrat to do so since [[2006 Kansas gubernatorial election|2006]]. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[Laura Kelly]] was term-limited and ineligible to seek a third consecutive term. Kansas was one of five Democratic-held [[Governor (United States)|governorships]] up for election in states [[Donald Trump]] carried in the [[2024 United States presidential election|2024 presidential election]]. Of these five, Kansas was the only state that Trump won by a double-digit margin, 57 percent to 41 percent. All five were successfully defended by the Democrats. ==Background== Kansas has a long tradition of ticket-splitting at the gubernatorial level as compared to presidential winners. Despite the state's consistent majority support for Republican presidential nominees, Democratic candidates won the governor's office in most of the years since the late 1960s, reflecting a pattern of voters distinguishing between state executive and federal races.{{cn|date=November 2026}} This competitive tradition continued in the [[2018 Kansas gubernatorial election|2018 election]], when Laura Kelly, a Kansas State Senator, won the open governor's seat in a favorable national environment during the [[2018 United States elections|2018 midterms]], and benefited from widespread dissatisfaction with the outgoing administration of [[Sam Brownback]], who had resigned in January 2018 after being confirmed by the Senate as [[United States Ambassador-at-Large for International Religious Freedom]], having been nominated for that position in July 2017.{{Cite news |last=Paul |first=Kari |date=November 7, 2018 |title=Kansas sees its own blue wave: 'If you can flip it here, you can flip it anywhere' |url=https://www.marketwatch.com/story/kansas-sees-its-own-blue-wave-if-you-can-flip-it-here-you-can-flip-it-anywhere-2018-11-07 |access-date=September 29, 2024 |work=[[MarketWatch]]}} Kelly won re-election in [[2022 Kansas gubernatorial election|2022]] on the strength of her own personal popularity, with the negative reaction to the [[Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization|overturning of ''Roe v. '''Minogue:''' {{legend0|#FFB2B2|40–50%}} {{legend0|#E27F7F|50–60%}} {{legend0|#D75D5D|60–70%}} | title = [[Governor of Massachusetts|Governor]] | before_election = [[Maura Healey]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Maura Healey]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) | last_update = 11:45 AM | time_zone = [[Eastern Time|ET]] }} {{ElectionsMA}} The '''2026 Massachusetts gubernatorial election''' was held on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Massachusetts]]. [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] incumbent [[Maura Healey]] won re-election to a second term, defeating [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] businessman Mike Minogue.{{Cite web |url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/11/03/us/elections/results-massachusetts-governor.html |title=Massachusetts Governor Election Results |work=[[Associated Press]] |via=[[The New York Times]] |access-date=November 4, 2026}} [[Primary elections]] took place on September 1, 2026, where Healey won the Democratic nomination running unopposed, while Minogue won the Republican nomination against Brian Shortsleeve.{{cite news|last=Shook|first=Ashley|date=September 22, 2025|title=Massachusetts legislature approves 2026 primary election date|url=https://www.wwlp.com/news/massachusetts/massachusetts-legislature-approves-2026-primary-election-date/|work=[[WWLP]]|access-date=September 24, 2025}}{{Cite web |last=Wolman |first=Jordan |date=2026-09-02 |title=Minogue wins GOP primary for governor, setting stage for matchup with Healey |url=https://commonwealthbeacon.org/politics/minogue-wins-gop-primary-for-governor-setting-stage-for-matchup-with-healey/ |access-date=2026-10-05 |website=CommonWealth Beacon |language=en-US}} In the run-up to the general election, Republican candidate Mike Minogue spent $6.1 million in September 2026 on his election bid, making it the most expensive gubernatorial race in Massachusetts history. Minogue outspent the 2006 Republican nominee and former Lieutenant Governor [[Kerry Healey]], who spent $4.4 million in the run-up to the [[2006 Massachusetts gubernatorial election|general election]] versus [[Deval Patrick]].{{Cite news |last=Buskirk |first=Chris Van |date=2026-10-02 |title=GOP nominee Michael Minogue spent a record $6.1 million last month |url=https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/10/02/metro/minogue-61-million-spending-september-governors-race/ |access-date=2026-10-05 |work=The Boston Globe |language=en-US |issn=0743-1791}} ==Democratic primary== === Governor === ==== Candidates ==== ===== Nominee ===== *[[Maura Healey]], incumbent governor (2023–present){{cite news |last1=Van Buskirk |first1=Chris |title=Massachusetts Gov. '''Cox:''' {{legend0|#FFB2B2|40–50%}} {{legend0|#E27F7F|50–60%}} {{legend0|#D75D5D|60–70%}} {{legend0|#D72F30|70–80%}} | title = [[Governor of Maryland|Governor]] | before_election = [[Wes Moore]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Wes Moore]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }}{{Elections in Maryland sidebar}} The '''2026 Maryland gubernatorial election''' took place on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Maryland]]. The primary elections took place on June 23, 2026.{{Cite web|date=May 9, 2025 |title=2026 State Primary Election Dates |url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|website= NCSL |access-date=August 5, 2025}} Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[Wes Moore]] was re-elected to a second term,{{cite news |last1=Wood |first1=Pamela |last2=Doyle |first2=Céilí |title=Wes Moore wins second term as Maryland governor |url=https://www.thebanner.com/politics-power/state-government/moore-governor-reelection-CII7U2KKMFESHIM4UHBGCYASDM/ |access-date=November 3, 2026 |work=[[The Baltimore Banner]] |date=November 3, 2026 |language=en}} defeating his [[2022 Maryland gubernatorial election|2022 opponent]] [[Dan Cox]]. This is the first gubernatorial rematch in Maryland since [[2010 Maryland gubernatorial election|2010]]. Moore is scheduled to serve a four-year term beginning on January 20, 2027.{{Cite web |title=Maryland Constitution – Article II, Section 1 |url=https://msa.maryland.gov/msa/mdmanual/43const/html/02art2.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260708215204/https://msa.maryland.gov/msa/mdmanual/43const/html/02art2.html |archive-date=July 8, 2026 |access-date=July 8, 2026 |website=msa.maryland.gov}} Despite Moore winning by an increased margin from 2022, Cox managed to flip two counties from the previous cycle, [[Kent County, Maryland|Kent]] and [[Talbot County, Maryland|Talbot]], both on the [[Eastern Shore of Maryland|Eastern Shore]].{{cite news |last1=Liu |first1=Sammy |title=Moore wins second term as Maryland voters approve redistricting amendment |url=https://cnsmaryland.org/2026/11/04/moore-wins-second-term-as-maryland-voters-approve-redistricting-amendment/ |access-date=November 23, 2026 |work=[[Capital News Service (Maryland)|Capital News Service]] |date=November 4, 2026}} Moore also garnered a lower vote share than the two other statewide candidates on the ballot, [[Brooke Lierman]] for [[2026 Maryland Comptroller election|Maryland Comptroller]] and [[Anthony Brown (Maryland politician)|Anthony Brown]] for [[2026 Maryland Attorney General election|Attorney General]].{{cite web |last1=Willis |first1=Derek |title=Introducing Skipjack |url=https://thescoop.org/archives/2026/11/25/introducing-skipjack/ |website=thescoop.org |access-date=November 25, 2026 |language=en |date=25 November 2026}} == Background == At the federal and state level, Maryland is a solid [[blue state]] and one of the most consistently Democratic states in the nation, with [[Kamala Harris]] carrying it by 29 points in the [[2024 United States presidential election in Maryland|2024 presidential election]]. Elections in Maryland are dominated by the [[Baltimore metropolitan area]] and the [[Washington metropolitan area|D.C. suburbs]].{{cite news |last1=Barker |first1=Jeff |title=Is Maryland growing even more blue politically? Democrats are showing gains in battleground counties. |url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2020/12/09/is-maryland-growing-even-more-blue-politically-democrats-are-showing-gains-in-battleground-counties/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241110030939/https://www.baltimoresun.com/2020/12/09/is-maryland-growing-even-more-blue-politically-democrats-are-showing-gains-in-battleground-counties/ |url-status=live |archive-date=November 10, 2024 |access-date=May 2, 2025 |work=[[The Baltimore Sun]] |url-access=subscription |date=December 9, 2020}} Going into this election, Democrats occupied all [[Government of Maryland#Executive branch|statewide offices]] and held supermajorities in both houses of the [[Maryland General Assembly|state legislature]], as well as all but one seat in the state's congressional delegation.{{cite news |last1=Schouten |first1=Fredreka |title=Wes Moore targets Maryland's only GOP congressman with redistricting, but a powerful Democrat stands in his way |url=https://www.cnn.com/2026/01/20/politics/maryland-redistricting-wes-moore |access-date=January 20, 2026 |work=[[CNN]] |date=January 20, 2026 |language=en}} == Democratic primary == === Campaign === Moore has maintained positive [[Governorship of Wes Moore#Approval ratings|approval ratings]] throughout his first term, though his numbers have steadily declined.{{cite news |last1=Janesch |first1=Sam |title=Gov. Wes Moore formally launches bid for second term |url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2025/09/09/gov-wes-moore-formally-launches-bid-for-second-term/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250909101141/https://www.baltimoresun.com/2025/09/09/gov-wes-moore-formally-launches-bid-for-second-term/ |url-status=live |archive-date=September 9, 2025 |access-date=September 9, 2025 |work=The Baltimore Sun |url-access=subscription |date=September 9, 2025}} Mileah Kromer, the director of the [[University of Maryland, Baltimore County]]'s Institute of Politics, has associated the downward trend in Moore's approval rating with voter frustration over affordability issues and a distrust of local, state, and federal government. An incumbent Democratic governor has not lost re-election in Maryland since [[1950 Maryland gubernatorial election|1950]], when [[William Preston Lane Jr.]] failed to win a second term. colspan=4 |Campaign finance reports as of June 7, 2026 |- style="text-align:center;" !Candidate !Raised !Spent !Cash on hand |- |{{party shading/Green}}|Andy Ellis (G) |$37,429 |$35,869 |$1,560 |- ! colspan="4" |Source: Maryland State Board of Elections |} ==General election== ===Campaign=== Moore was widely expected to win re-election to a second term and entered the general election with a substantial fundraising advantage over Cox.{{cite news |last1=Ibrahim |first1=Mennatalla |title=Ed Hale concedes to Dan Cox in Maryland GOP governor primary race |url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2026/06/23/early-returns-show-hale-cox-locked-in-tight-maryland-gop-governor-race/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260624112931/https://www.baltimoresun.com/2026/06/23/early-returns-show-hale-cox-locked-in-tight-maryland-gop-governor-race/ |url-status=live |archive-date=June 24, 2026 |access-date=June 24, 2026 |work=[[The Baltimore Sun]] |url-access=subscription |date=June 23, 2026}} Moore campaigned on his efforts to address affordability issues, expand opportunities, and protect the state from the [[second Trump administration]], whose actions have led to increased prices and caused the state to lose jobs and federal funding. Moore's campaign also sought to tie Cox to President [[Donald Trump]], who endorsed Cox in [[2022 Maryland gubernatorial election|2022]].{{cite news |last1=Wood |first1=Pamela |title=Governor rematch: Democrat Moore will face GOP's Cox again |url=https://www.thebanner.com/politics-power/maryland-governor-primary-election-2026-BBC7RVV2FBAMBBNS6UZR2I27WM/ |access-date=June 24, 2026 |work=[[The Baltimore Banner]] |date=June 23, 2026 |language=en}} Following the primary elections, the [[Maryland Democratic Party]] launched a website intended to remind voters about Cox's association with Trump as well as his past opposition to abortion rights, gun safety, and former President [[Joe Biden]]'s victory in the [[2020 United States presidential election]]. Cox pushed back against attempts to tie him to Trump, saying that he would not be seeking the president's endorsement and would be focusing his campaign on local issues.{{cite news |title=Republican nominee Dan Cox bites back at Gov. Moore on Maryland redistricting |url=https://wtop.com/maryland/2026/07/republican-nominee-dan-cox-bites-back-at-gov-moore-on-maryland-redistricting/ |access-date=July 1, 2026 |work=[[WTOP-FM]] |date=July 1, 2026}} Cox campaigned against Moore's handling of economic issues. Following the Republican primary, the [[Maryland Republican Party]] and its leaders embraced Cox,{{cite news |last1=Chingarande |first1=Tinashe |title=Dan Cox says Maryland affordability crisis gives GOP new opening in 2026 |url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2026/07/08/dan-cox-says-maryland-affordability-crisis-gives-gop-new-opening-in-2026/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260708093259/https://www.baltimoresun.com/2026/07/08/dan-cox-says-maryland-affordability-crisis-gives-gop-new-opening-in-2026/ |url-status=live |archive-date=July 8, 2026 |access-date=July 8, 2026 |work=[[The Baltimore Sun]] |url-access=subscription |date=July 8, 2026}} with [[Maryland Senate]] minority leader [[Steve Hershey]] and [[Maryland House of Delegates|House of Delegates]] minority leader [[Jason C. Buckel]] telling ''[[The Baltimore Sun]]'' that they believed Cox could defeat Moore with an affordability-focused campaign as opposed to 2022 campaign platform, which highlighted far-right policy stances and baseless conspiracy theories. '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#d2b1d9|40–50%}} | map_size = | title = [[Governor of Maine|Governor]] | before_election = [[Janet Mills]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Hannah Pingree]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsME}} The '''2026 Maine gubernatorial election''' took place on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Maine]]. Democrat [[Hannah Pingree]] defeated Republican lawyer [[Robert B. Charles|Bobby Charles]] and independent [[Rick Bennett (Maine politician)|Rick Bennett]].{{cite web|last=Goodwin|first=Liz|title=Democrat Hannah Pingree wins Maine governor's race, will succeed Janet Mills|publisher=The Washington Post|date=November 3, 2026|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/elections/results/2026/11/03/maine-governor-charles-pingree-live-updates/|access-date=November 4, 2026}}{{cite web|last=Reed|first=Russ|title=Maine gubernatorial election results: AP calls race for Democrat Hannah Pingree|publisher=WMTW|date=November 3, 2026|url=https://www.wmtw.com/article/maine-governor-election-results-2026-charles-pingree-bennett/74295736|access-date=November 4, 2026}} Incumbent [[Maine Democratic Party|Democratic]] governor [[Janet Mills]] was [[Term limits in the United States|ineligible]] to seek re-election to a third consecutive term. Although Maine has adopted [[Instant-runoff voting|ranked-choice voting]], it is only used for primary elections and federal general elections. Therefore, the primary was conducted with ranked-choice voting, and the general election was conducted with the traditional [[Plurality voting|plurality voting]] system. [[Primary elections]] were held on June 9, 2026.{{Cite web |title=2026 State Primary Election Dates |url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates |access-date=2025-05-23 |website=[[National Conference of State Legislatures]]}} This was the first Maine gubernatorial election since [[1952 Maine gubernatorial election|1952]] where the elected governor was a member of the same political party as the outgoing governor.{{Cite web |date=2026-11-04 |title=Hannah Pingree wins Maine governor’s race |url=https://www.pressherald.com/2026/11/03/hannah-pingree-is-favored-in-the-maine-governors-race-now-results-are-coming-in/ |access-date=2026-11-07 |website=The Portland Press Herald |language=en-US}} == Background == Incumbent Democratic governor [[Janet Mills]] was re-elected with 55.69% of the vote in [[2022 Maine gubernatorial election|2022]] over Republican former governor [[Paul LePage]].{{Cite news |last=Mistler |first=Steve |date=2022-11-09 |title=Maine Gov. Janet Mills wins second term, defeating former GOP Gov. Paul LePage |url=https://www.npr.org/2022/11/09/1134198072/maine-election-results-governor-paul-lepage-janet-mills |access-date=2026-01-20 |work=NPR |language=en}} She is term-limited and not eligible to run for a third consecutive term. A sparsely populated state in [[New England]], Maine is one of the most [[Rural areas in the United States|rural]] states in the nation and is considered to be moderately [[Red states and blue states|blue]]. Both houses of the [[Maine Legislature]] were controlled by the Maine Democratic Party in the prior session. A Republican has not received 50% or more of the vote in a gubernatorial election since [[1962 Maine gubernatorial election|1962]], when incumbent Republican [[John H. Reed]] received 50.08% of the vote.{{Cite web |title=Maine Election Returns |url=https://www.maine.gov/legis/lawlib/lldl/elections/electionshome.html |access-date=2026-01-20 |website=www.maine.gov}} ==Democratic primary== [[Shenna Bellows]], [[Troy Jackson]], and [[Hannah Pingree]] announced an "alliance" on May 22, 2026, in which they would rank each other ahead of their opponents [[Angus King III]] and [[Nirav D. Shah|Nirav Shah]]; Shah was leading in most public polls.{{Cite web |last=Brodey |first=Sam |date=May 28, 2026 |title=It has famous names, wildcards, and a COVID doctor: How Maine's governor race became the primary to watch - The Boston Globe |url=https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/05/28/nation/maine-janet-mills-governor-race-graham-platner/ |access-date=2026-05-28 |website=BostonGlobe.com |language=en-US}} Shah received the most first-preference votes, with 26.8%, followed by Pingree with 23.3%, Jackson with 21.0%, Bellows with 20.7%, and King with 8.2%. As a result of finishing last, King was eliminated and his voters' second preferences were redistributed to the remaining four candidates. Pingree was ultimately nominated after four rounds of ranked-choice tabulation, defeating Shah in the final round by a 56%–44% margin.{{Cite web |date=2026-06-19 |title=Hannah Pingree wins ranked-choice runoff in Democratic primary for governor |url=https://www.pressherald.com/2026/06/19/hannah-pingree-wins-ranked-choice-runoff-in-democratic-primary-for-governor/ |access-date=2026-06-19 |website=The Portland Press Herald |language=en-US}} Following his loss in the gubernatorial primary, Jackson became the Democratic nominee in the [[2026 United States Senate election in Maine|2026 [[Robert B. Charles|Robert Charles]] was particularly critical of ranked choice voting and encouraged Republican primary voters to rank him across the ballot and not rank other candidates. Charles criticized what he called "back room deals" among other candidates to encourage their supporters to rank another candidate second, claiming other candidates could not be trusted to work to repeal ranked choice voting while encouraging its use.{{Cite web |last=Mistler |first=Steve |date=2026-05-15 |title=Looking to topple Bobby Charles, Maine's GOP primary candidates are turning to an unlikely tool |url=https://www.mainepublic.org/politics/2026-05-15/looking-to-topple-bobby-charles-maines-gop-primary-candidates-are-turning-to-an-unlikely-tool|access-date=2025-05-19 |website=[[MPBN]] |language=en-US}}{{Cite web |last=Miller |first=Kevin |date=2026-05-08 |title=Some, but not all, GOP gubernatorial candidates are embracing ranked-choice voting |url=https://www.mainepublic.org/politics/2026-05-08/some-but-not-all-gop-gubernatorial-candidates-are-embracing-ranked-choice-voting|access-date=2025-05-19 |website=[[MPBN]] |language=en-US}} The candidates who endorsed a second choice were Robert Wessels, who endorsed [[Jonathan S. colspan="4" |Source: Maine Ethics Commission |} == General election == Pingree maintained a large polling and fundraising lead for the duration of the campaign, with just a single poll showing her with less than an eight-point lead. She also received the endorsements of several prominent Republicans and independents, including senator [[Angus King]]. In September, Charles came under fire from his sister Anita, who criticized his stance on abortion rights and his relationship with former U.S. House Speaker [[Dennis Hastert]], who in 2016 was convicted for financial crimes related to his alleged abuse of teenage boys.{{Cite web |date=2026-09-09 |title=I'm Bobby Charles' sister. I'm voting for Hannah Pingree. |url=https://www.pressherald.com/2026/09/09/im-bobby-charles-sister-im-voting-for-hannah-pingree-opinion/ |access-date=2026-11-07 |website=The Portland Press Herald |language=en-US}}{{Cite news |last=Davey |first=Monica |last2=Smith |first2=Mitch |date=2016-04-09 |title=Hastert Molested at Least Four Boys, Prosecutors Say |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/04/09/us/dennis-hastert-molested-at-least-four-boys-prosecutors-say.html |access-date=2026-11-08 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} Anita Charles said she would be supporting Pingree. In October, the Charles campaign was fined over $22,000 by the Maine Ethics Commission for campaign donation violations.{{Cite web |date=2026-10-26|title=Bobby Charles fined more than $22,000 for Maine gubernatorial campaign donation violations|url=https://www.pressherald.com/2026/10/26/bobby-charles-fined-more-than-22000-for-maine-gubernatorial-campaign-donation-violations/|access-date=2026-10-27|website=The Portland Press Herald|language=en-US}} Charles, whose campaign was considered bellicose in the Republican primary,{{Cite web |last=Romans |first=Payton |date=2026-08-18 |title=Are Maine political campaigns required to disclose when they use AI in ads? |url=https://wgme.com/news/i-team/are-maine-political-campaigns-required-to-disclose-when-they-use-ai-in-ads |access-date=2026-11-08 |website=WGME |language=en}} opted for a more low-key campaign style during the general election, holding an open forum where anyone could ask him questions at the [[Auburn Mall (Maine)|Auburn Mall]] on the eve of the election.{{Cite web |date=2026-10-30 |title=In Auburn, Bobby Charles wanted to be challenged. Here’s how it went. |url=https://www.pressherald.com/2026/10/29/at-his-auburn-mall-event-bobby-charles-wanted-to-be-challenged-heres-how-it-went/ |access-date=2026-11-08 |website=The Portland Press Herald |language=en-US}} On election day, Pingree defeated Charles by 17 points, the largest margin of victory for a first-term gubernatorial candidate since Republican [[Frederick G. Payne]] defeated Democrat [[Louis Lausier]] by 31 points in [[1948 Maine gubernatorial election|1948]], and Pingree's 54.4% of the vote is the most a first-term gubernatorial candidate since Payne received 65.6% of the vote in that election.{{Cite web |title=Maine Election Results by Town, 1820–2026 |url=https://mainepoliticaldata.com/election-results/ |access-date=2026-11-08 |website=Maine Political Data |language=en}} Pingree became the first governor to succeed a governor of the same party since [[Burton M. Cross]], a Republican, who would be elected to succeed Payne in [[1952 Maine gubernatorial election|1952]].{{Cite web |date=2026-11-04 |title=Hannah Pingree wins Maine governor’s race |url=https://www.pressherald.com/2026/11/03/hannah-pingree-is-favored-in-the-maine-governors-race-now-results-are-coming-in/ |access-date=2026-11-07 |website=The Portland Press Herald |language=en-US}} Pingree's margin of victory was the largest for any Maine governor since Angus King won the [[1998 Maine gubernatorial election|1998 election]] by nearly 40 points.{{Cite web |date=2022-11-10 |title=How Maine voted: Governor’s races 1990 – 2022 |url=https://www.pressherald.com/2022/11/10/how-maine-voted-governors-races-1990-2022/ |access-date=2026-11-08 |website=The Portland Press Herald |language=en-US}} The 37.4% of the vote Charles received is the worst result for a Republican gubernatorial candidate since [[Chandler Woodcock]] received 30.2% in [[2006 Maine gubernatorial election|2006]]. Bennett's 8.1% of the vote is the best showing for an independent candidate since [[Eliot Cutler]] received 8.4% of the vote in [[2014 Maine gubernatorial election|2014]]. Despite performing worse in the popular vote than [[2022 Maine gubernatorial election|2022]] nominee [[Paul LePage]], Charles did manage to flip [[Franklin County, Maine|Franklin County]]. It had supported Democrat [[Janet Mills]], who is a native of Franklin County, in [[2018 Maine gubernatorial election|2018]] and 2022. Pingree flipped [[Androscoggin County, Maine|Androscoggin County]], which had last voted for a Democratic gubernatorial candidate in [[2006 Maine gubernatorial election|2006]] and had voted Republican in each subsequent election. It had last voted for a Democrat in any statewide election in 2012, when it voted for [[Barack Obama]] in [[2012 United States presidential election in Maine|that year's presidential election]]. '''James:''' {{legend0|#FFB2B2|40–50%}} {{legend0|#E27F7F|50–60%}} {{legend0|#D75D5D|60–70%}} {{legend0|#D72F30|70–80%}} | title = [[Governor of Michigan|Governor]] | before_election = [[Gretchen Whitmer]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Jocelyn Benson]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsMI}} The '''2026 Michigan gubernatorial election''' was held on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Michigan]]. [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] state secretary of state [[Jocelyn Benson]] defeated [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] representative [[John James (Michigan politician)|John James]]. Democratic incumbent [[Gretchen Whitmer]] was ineligible to seek a third term. [[Primary elections]] were held on August 4. Benson won the Democratic nomination with 83.2% of the vote over Genesee County Sheriff Chris Swanson. Endorsed by President [[Donald Trump]], James won the Republican nomination with 50.1% of the vote over businessman [[Perry Johnson (businessman)|Perry Johnson]]. Republicans had not won a gubernatorial election in Michigan since [[2014 Michigan gubernatorial election|2014]]. This was the first gubernatorial election in Michigan since [[1960 Michigan gubernatorial election|1960]] in which a Democrat who was not the incumbent governor was elected while there was an incumbent Democratic governor. This was also the first time since [[1998 Michigan gubernatorial election|1998]] that either major party won the Michigan governorship in more than two consecutive elections, and the first time Democrats did so since [[1960 Michigan gubernatorial election|1960]]. {{toclimit|3}} ==Background== Michigan is a [[Swing state|purple]] state in the heart of the [[Great Lakes]] and [[Rust Belt]] which consistently elected [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrats]] for president since [[1992 United States presidential election in Michigan|1992]] until [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] nominee [[Donald Trump]] narrowly flipped the state in [[2016 United States presidential election in Michigan|2016]]. In [[2020 United States presidential election in Michigan|2020]], Democratic nominee [[Joe Biden]] won Michigan by 2.78%. In the [[2024 United States presidential election in Michigan|2024 presidential election]], Donald Trump won Michigan by 1.42%, which was attributed to [[Joe Biden|President Biden]]'s unpopularity and rightward shifts in working-class and [[Arab Americans|Arab American]] voters.{{Cite web |title=Michigan Presidential Election Voting History - 270toWin |url=https://www.270towin.com/states/michigan |access-date=2025-09-07 |website=270toWin.com}}{{Cite news |last=Shalal |first=Andrea |date=November 10, 2024 |title=Kamala Harris' Michigan loss highlights Democrats' weak spots |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/us/harris-michigan-loss-highlights-democrats-many-weak-spots-2024-11-10/ |access-date=January 1, 2026 |work=[[Reuters]]}} Since the [[2018 Michigan elections]], Democrats occupied all statewide offices in Michigan. Since [[2022 Michigan Senate election|2022]], Democrats held a narrow majority in the [[Michigan Senate|State Senate]] while Republicans held a narrow majority in the [[Michigan House of Representatives]] since [[2024 Michigan House of Representatives election|2024]]. According to the [[Morning Consult]], which measures the popularity of governors across the country, Democratic governor [[Gretchen Whitmer]] has a net +26 approval rating in Michigan as of September 2026.{{Cite web |date=February 2, 2026 |title=Tracking the Approval Ratings of All 50 U.S. Governors |url=https://pro.morningconsult.com/trackers/governor-approval-ratings |access-date=September 24, 2026 |website=[[Morning Consult]]}} In [[2018 Michigan gubernatorial election|2018]], Gretchen Whitmer and her running mate [[Garlin Gilchrist]] won by 9.56%. '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#D2B1D9|40–50%}} {{legend0|#AE8BB1|50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No votes}} | title = [[Governor of Minnesota|Governor]] | before_election = [[Tim Walz]] | before_party = Minnesota Democratic–Farmer–Labor Party | after_election = [[Amy Klobuchar]] | after_party = Minnesota Democratic–Farmer–Labor Party | last_update = 12:47 PM | time_zone = [[Central time|CT]] }} {{ElectionsMN}} The '''2026 Minnesota gubernatorial election''' was held on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Minnesota|governor]] and [[Lieutenant Governor of Minnesota|lieutenant governor]] of [[Minnesota]]. [[Minnesota Democratic–Farmer–Labor Party|Democratic]] senator [[Amy Klobuchar]] defeated [[Republican Party of Minnesota|Republican]] state House speaker [[Lisa Demuth]] in the general election. Democratic incumbent [[Tim Walz]] initially ran for a third term, but withdrew in January following a [[2020s Minnesota fraud scandals|scandal over fraud in state funded-social services]]. Following Walz's withdrawal, Klobuchar entered the Democratic primary and won the nomination with 89.7% of the vote against minimal opposition. In the Republican primary, Demuth defeated businessman [[Mike Lindell]], who was endorsed by President [[Donald Trump]], and healthcare technology executive Kendall Qualls, who was endorsed by the state party, with 43.4% of the vote. With her victory, Klobuchar will become the first female governor of Minnesota.{{Cite web |last=Akaolisa |first=Tom |date=2026-08-17 |title=MINNEAPOLIMEDIA EDITORIAL {{!}} Minnesota Will Elect Its First Woman Governor. '''Walz:''' {{legend0|#a5b0ff|40–50%}} {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} }} {{Elections in Nebraska}} The '''2026 Nebraska gubernatorial election''' was held on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Nebraska]]. Incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] governor [[Jim Pillen]] won re-election to a second term. [[Primary elections]] took place on May 12, 2026.{{Cite web|date=May 9, 2025|title=2026 State Primary Election Dates|url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260509222424/https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|archive-date=May 9, 2026|website=way[[National Conference of State Legislatures]]|access-date=August 5, 2025}} Pillen secured his party's nomination with 76% of the vote, while [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] former state senator [[Lynne Walz]] secured her party's nomination with 91% of the vote. This was the best performance for a Democrat in a Nebraska gubernatorial election since [[1994 Nebraska gubernatorial election|1994]], which was also the most recent time that Democrats won a gubernatorial election in Nebraska. '''Warmington:''' {{legend0|#a5b0ff|40–50%}} {{legend0|#7996E2|50–60%}} | map_image = {{switcher |[[File:2026 New Hampshire gubernatorial election results map by county.svg|x240px]] |County results|[[File:2022 New Hampshire gubernatorial election results map by congressional district.svg|x240px]] |Congressional district results}} }} {{Elections in New Hampshire}} The '''2026 New Hampshire gubernatorial election''' was held on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[Governor of New Hampshire|governor]] of the [[U.S. state]] of [[New Hampshire]]. Incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] governor [[Kelly Ayotte]] defeated Democrat [[Cinde Warmington]], winning re-election to a second two-year term in office.{{cite web|last1=Rogers|first1=Josh|last2=Harris|first2=Jackie|title=Ayotte secures reelection, providing a rare bright spot for NH Republicans|publisher=NHPR New Hampshire Public Radio|date=November 4, 2026|url=https://www.nhpr.org/nh-news/2026-11-04/governor-nh-newhampshire-election-ayotte|access-date=November 4, 2026}} The primary elections took place on September 8, 2026.{{Cite web|date=May 9, 2025 |title=2026 State Primary Election Dates |url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|website= NCSL |access-date=5 August 2025}} Along with neighboring [[2026 Vermont gubernatorial election|Vermont]], it was one of two Republican-held governorships up for election in a state that [[Kamala Harris]] won in the [[2024 United States presidential election|2024 presidential election]]. New Hampshire was one of two states to vote for different parties for Senate and governor in 2026, electing a Republican governor and a Democratic senator ([[Chris Pappas (American politician)|Chris Pappas]], in the [[2026 United States Senate election in New Hampshire|concurrent Senate election]]). The other one was South Carolina, which also elected a Republican governor ([[Alan Wilson (politician)|Alan Wilson]], in the [[2026 South Carolina gubernatorial election]]), and a Democratic senator ([[Annie Andrews]], in the [[2026 United States Senate election in South Carolina|concurrent Senate election]]). == Background == New Hampshire has voted [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] in each presidential race starting in [[2004 United States presidential election in New Hampshire|2004]]. The state's congressional delegation has been entirely Democratic since 2017. Conversely, Republicans hold a trifecta on the statewide level, with a supermajority in the [[New Hampshire Senate]].{{Cite news |last=Cullen |first=Margie |date=November 7, 2024 |title=NH keeps GOP in control of state while voting for Democrats in D.C. Experts explain why. |url=https://www.seacoastonline.com/story/news/politics/elections/2024/11/07/nh-voters-republicans-state-government-democrats-washington/76085089007/ |url-status=live |archive-date=November 7, 2024 |access-date=January 17, 2026 |work=[[Portsmouth Herald]]}} In [[2024 New Hampshire gubernatorial election|2024]], [[Kelly Ayotte]] won the gubernatorial election by '''Hull:''' {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}} {{legend0|#d72f30|70–80%}} | before_election = [[Michelle Lujan Grisham]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = '''[[Deb Haaland]]''' | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsNM}} The '''2026 New Mexico gubernatorial election''' was held on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of New Mexico]]. [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] former [[United States Secretary of the Interior|U.S. secretary of the interior]] [[Deb Haaland]] defeated [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] former [[Rio Rancho, New Mexico|Rio Rancho]] mayor [[Gregg Hull]] in the general election. Democratic incumbent [[Michelle Lujan Grisham]] was [[Term limits in the United States|term-limited]] and ineligible to seek a third consecutive term. [[Primary elections]] took place on June 2. Haaland defeated [[Bernalillo County, New Mexico|Bernalillo County]] district attorney Sam Bregman in the Democratic primary with 72% of the vote. Hull defeated Doug Turner and Duke Rodriguez in the Republican primary with 47% of the vote. This election was the first New Mexico gubernatorial election since [[1978 New Mexico gubernatorial election|1978]] in which either party won the governorship for three consecutive terms. ==Democratic 2026 Nevada gubernatorial election.text:
{{short description|none}} {{for|related races|2026 United States gubernatorial elections}} {{Use American English|date=January 2025}} {{Use mdy dates|date=November 2024}} {{Infobox election | election_name = 2026 Nevada gubernatorial election | country = Nevada | type = presidential | ongoing = no | previous_election = 2022 Nevada gubernatorial election | previous_year = 2022 | next_election = 2030 Nevada gubernatorial election | next_year = 2030 | election_date = November 3, 2026 | image1 = Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford addresses the United Nations Human Rights Committee, October 17-18, 2023 1 (cropped).jpg | nominee1 = '''[[Aaron Ford]]''' | running_mate1 = | party1 = Democratic Party (United States) | popular_vote1 = '''568,433''' | percentage1 = '''51.72%''' | image2 = Joe Lombardo (55512471876) (cropped).jpg | nominee2 = [[Joe Lombardo]] | party2 = Republican Party (United States) | running_mate2 = | popular_vote2 = 482,325 | percentage2 = 43.89% | title = [[Governor of Nevada|Governor]] | before_election = [[Joe Lombardo]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Aaron Ford]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) | map_image = {{switcher |[[File:2026 Nevada gubernatorial election results map by county.svg|250px]] |County results |[[File:2022 United States Senate election in Nevada results map by congressional district.svg|250px]] |Congressional district results}} | map_size = 250px | map_caption = '''Ford:''' {{legend0|#7996E2|50–60%}}
'''Lombardo:''' {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}} {{legend0|#d72f30|70–80%}} {{legend0|#C21B18|80-90%}} }} {{ElectionsNV}} The '''2026 Nevada gubernatorial election''' was held on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Nevada]]. [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] incumbent [[Joe Lombardo]] sought re-election to a second term, but lost to [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] attorney general [[Aaron Ford]]. [[Primary elections]] took place on June 9, 2026.{{Cite web|date=May 9, 2025|title=2026 State Primary Election Dates|url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|website=[[National Conference of State Legislatures]]|access-date=August 5, 2025}} Lombardo won the Republican nomination with 91.0% of the vote. Ford won the Democratic nomination with 63.8% over Washoe commission chair [[Alexis Hill (Nevada politician)|Alexis Hill]]. Lombardo is the second consecutive governor of Nevada to lose re-election after [[Steve Sisolak]] in 2022. Ford became Nevada's first African American governor and the first Black person elected governor of a U.S. state west of the Mississippi River. Lombardo was one of two Republican governors to lose re-election in 2026, the other one being [[Greg Abbott]] in [[2026 Texas gubernatorial election|Texas]]. == Background == Nevada is considered to be a purple to slightly blue state at the federal and state levels, with neither party having [[Government trifecta|control of all three]] branches of government. Apart from the governor, Nevada's [[Lieutenant Governor of Nevada|lieutenant governor]] and [[Nevada State Controller|state controller]] are Republicans. Nevada's [[Nevada Attorney General|attorney general]], [[Nevada State Treasurer|treasurer]], and [[Secretary of State of Nevada|state secretary of state]] are Democrats.{{Cite web |title=Party control of Nevada state government |url=https://ballotpedia.org/Party_control_of_Nevada_state_government |access-date=2026-11-17 |website=[[Ballotpedia]] |language=en}} [[Donald Trump]] won the state in [[2024 United States presidential election|2024]], becoming the first Republican presidential nominee to win the state since [[2004 United States presidential election in Nevada|2004]].{{cite news |title=Trump turns Nevada red in presidential race for first time in two decades |url=https://abc3340.com/news/nation-world/trump-turns-nevada-red-in-presidential-race-for-first-time-in-two-decades |access-date=March 6, 2026 |publisher=ABC3340 |date=November 6, 2024}} The [[Nevada Legislature]] is controlled by members of the Democratic Party, with a majority in both the [[Nevada Assembly|state assembly]] and [[Nevada Senate|senate]]. The lieutenant governor, a Republican, serves as the president of the state senate but only votes in the case of a tie. At the federal level, both [[United States Senate|United States Senators]] and three out of four members of the [[United States House of Representatives]] from Nevada are Democrats.{{Cite news |title=Election Results, 2022 |url=https://www.reviewjournal.com/election-results-2022/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221123004555/https://www.reviewjournal.com/election-results-2022/ |archive-date=November 23, 2022 |work=[[Las Vegas Review-Journal]]}}{{Cite news |title=Election Results, 2024 |url=https://www.reviewjournal.com/general-election-results-2024/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241229090710/https://www.reviewjournal.com/general-election-results-2024/ |archive-date=December 29, 2024 |work=[[Las Vegas Review-Journal]]}} With the exception of [[2018 Nevada gubernatorial election|2018]], Republicans have won every gubernatorial election in the state since [[1998 Nevada gubernatorial election|1998]].{{Cite news |last1=Mueller |first1=Tabitha |last2=Golonka |first2=Sean |last3=Solis |first3=Jacob |date=November 11, 2022 |title=Lombardo defeats Sisolak; '''Blakeman:''' {{legend0|#ffb2b2|40–50%}} {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}} {{legend0|#d72f30|70–80%}} | title = [[Governor of New York|Governor]] | before_election = [[Kathy Hochul]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Kathy Hochul]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }}{{ElectionsNY}} The '''2026 New York gubernatorial election''' took place on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of New York]]. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[Kathy Hochul]] ran for re-election to a second full term.{{Cite news |last=Parsnow |first=Luke |date=July 2, 2024 |title=Hochul says she's running for another term as New York governor in 2026 |url=https://spectrumlocalnews.com/nys/central-ny/politics/2024/07/02/hochul-says-she-s-running-for-another-term-as-governor-in-2026 |access-date=August 20, 2024 |website=[[Spectrum News]] |language=en |archive-date=July 8, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240708215410/https://spectrumlocalnews.com/nys/central-ny/politics/2024/07/02/hochul-says-she-s-running-for-another-term-as-governor-in-2026 |url-status=live}} [[Primary elections]] took place on June 23, 2026.{{Cite web|date=May 9, 2025|title=2026 State Primary Election Dates|url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260423040741/https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|archive-date=April 23, 2026|access-date=August 5, 2025|website=[[National Conference of State Legislatures|NCSL]]}} The gubernatorial candidates selected their running mates, instead of having separate primaries.{{cite news|last=Cuza|first=Bobby|date=May 8, 2025|title=State lawmakers eliminate lieutenant governor primary|url=https://ny1.com/nyc/all-boroughs/politics/2025/05/09/albany-lawmakers-eliminate-lieutenant-governor-primary?cid=share_clip|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260105102847/https://ny1.com/nyc/all-boroughs/politics/2025/05/09/albany-lawmakers-eliminate-lieutenant-governor-primary?cid=share_clip|archive-date=January 5, 2026|work=[[Spectrum News]] |url-status=live}} Kathy Hochul faced Nassau County executive [[Bruce Blakeman]], the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] and [[Conservative Party of New York State|Conservative]] nominee, in the general election. After U.S. representative [[Elise Stefanik]] withdrew from the Republican primary in December 2025, Blakeman was endorsed by President [[Donald Trump]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.politico.com/news/2025/12/20/trump-new-york-governor-endorsement-bruce-blakeman-00702013|title=Trump endorses in New York governor race the day after Stefanik drops out|date=December 20, 2025|work=Politico|access-date=2026-10-10}} Republicans have not won a statewide election in New York since [[George Pataki]] was re-elected governor in [[2002 New York gubernatorial election|2002]].{{Cite news|url=https://abc7ny.com/post/new-york-rep-elise-stefanik-announce-run-governor-soon-friday/18122558/|title=Rep. Elise Stefanik to announce run for New York governor as soon as Friday|date=November 6, 2025|work=ABC7 New York|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251107000827/https://abc7ny.com/post/new-york-rep-elise-stefanik-announce-run-governor-soon-friday/18122558/|archive-date=2025-11-07|access-date=2026-10-10|url-status=live}} On Election Day, Hochul won her second full term in office, defeating Blakeman. Her margin of victory improved from the previous election, powered by sweeping gains in [[Downstate New York]]. This included narrow victories for Hochul in both of [[Long Island|Long Island's]] suburban counties of [[Suffolk County, New York|Suffolk]] and [[Nassau County, New York|Nassau]], the later of which was Blakeman's home county and where he has served as [[county executive]] since 2022. ==Background== Governor [[Kathy Hochul]] took office on August 24, 2021, upon the resignation of her predecessor, [[Andrew Cuomo]].{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/08/24/nyregion/kathy-hochul-governor-ny.html|title=Hochul Is Sworn In: 'I Want People to Believe in Their Government Again'|first=Luis|last=Ferré-Sadurní|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=August 24, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211224074148/https://www.nytimes.com/2021/08/24/nyregion/kathy-hochul-governor-ny.html|archive-date=2021-12-24|access-date=2026-10-10|url-status=live}} Hochul was elected to a full term in [[2022 New York gubernatorial election|2022]] with 53.1% of the vote in the closest New York gubernatorial election since [[1994 New York gubernatorial election|1994]].{{cite web |title=2022 General Election Governor and Lt. Because New York utilizes a fusion voting system, Blakeman accepted the third-party ballot line to run concurrently on both the Republican and Conservative lines.{{cite news |title=Bruce Blakeman receives nomination for governor from NY State Conservative Party |url=https://longisland.news12.com/bruce-blakeman-receives-nomination-for-governor-from-ny-state-conservative-party |work=News 12 |access-date=2026-02-15}} ===Candidates=== ====Nominee==== *[[Bruce Blakeman]], [[Nassau County Executive|Nassau County executive]] (2021–present) **Running mate: Todd Hood, [[Madison County, New York|Madison County]] sheriff (2018–present) ==Working Families convention== The [[Working Families Party|New York Working Families Party]] declined to nominate Hochul or Delgado, instead opting for a "placeholder candidate" to appear on their ballot line. The party has stated that the placeholder candidate will later be replaced by the Democratic nominee. A convention attendee told ''[[City & State]]'' that Delgado won 41% of the weighted party committee vote to Hochul's 3%, while "placeholder candidate" won 56% of the vote. State party leaders Jasmine Gripper and [[Ana María Archila]] disputed the claim, but did not share the exact vote totals. On August 21, the Working Families Party nominated Hochul and Adams. ===Candidates=== ====Nominee==== *[[Kathy Hochul]], [[governor of New York]] (2021–present){{Cite news |last1=Kaufman |first1=Maya |date=2026-08-21 |url=https://www.politico.com/newsletters/new-york-playbook-pm/2026/08/21/city-halls-next-big-pay-dilemma-01046007 |title=City Hall’s next big pay dilemma |access-date=2026-10-10 |work=Politico |language=en-US}} **Running mate: [[Adrienne Adams (politician)|Adrienne Adams]], former speaker of the [[New York City Council]] (2022–2025) from the [[New York City's 28th City Council district|28th district]] (2017–2025) and candidate for [[mayor of New York City]] in [[2025 New York City mayoral election|2025]] == Independents and other parties == The [[New York State Board of Elections]] rejected all petitions for non-qualified party ballot access in May 2026.{{cite web |title=2026 General Prima Facie and Hearing Report |url=https://elections.ny.gov/2026-general-prima-facie-and-hearing-report |website=New York State Board of Elections |date=June 4, 2026 |access-date=June 26, 2026}} ===Libertarian Party=== The [[Libertarian Party of New York]] (LPNY) had no ballot line in 2026, having lost ballot access after the 2020 state budget raised the qualification thresholds.{{cite press release |title=NY Libertarians Urge Voters to Write In "None of the Above" for Governor, Reject Hochul and Blakeman |url=https://lpny.org/2026/10/24/ny-libertarians-urge-voters-to-write-in-none-of-the-above-for-governor-reject-hochul-and-blakeman/ |publisher=Libertarian Party of New York |date=October 24, 2026 |access-date=November 4, 2026}} At its nominating convention in [[Rochester, New York|Rochester]] on October 25, 2025, the party's State Committee nominated [[Larry Sharpe (political activist)|Larry Sharpe]],{{cite news |last=Day |first=Lucas |date=October 27, 2025 |title=Larry Sharpe Nominated as Libertarian Candidate for Governor |url=https://www.fingerlakesdailynews.com/regional-state-congressional/larry-sharpe-nominated-as-libertarian-candidate-for-governor/ |work=Finger Lakes Daily News |access-date=November 7, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251101003648/https://www.fingerlakesdailynews.com/regional-state-congressional/larry-sharpe-nominated-as-libertarian-candidate-for-governor/|archive-date=2025-11-01|url-status=live}} its 2018 and 2022 candidate, for governor, giving him 12 of 20 votes over Christopher Olenski and "None of the Above" (NOTA). Nominations for lieutenant governor and the other statewide offices were postponed.{{cite web |title=Minutes of the Meeting of the State Committee, October 25, 2025 |url=https://mywikis-wiki-media.s3.us-central-1.wasabisys.com/lpedia/LPNY_MINUTES_2025-10-25_APPROVED_2026-09-27.pdf |publisher=Libertarian Party of New York |access-date=November 4, 2026}} In February 2026, Sharpe announced a campaign for the [[Republican Party of New York|Republican]] nomination to challenge Nassau County Executive [[Bruce Blakeman]], urging registered Libertarians to switch their enrollment so they could vote in the closed primary.{{cite news |last=Parsnow |first=Luke |title=Libertarian Larry Sharpe enters Republican primary for New York governor |url=https://spectrumlocalnews.com/nys/central-ny/politics/2026/02/06/libertarian-larry-sharpe-enters-republican-primary-for-new-york-governor |work=Spectrum News 1 |date=February 6, 2026 |access-date=November 4, 2026}} Sharpe himself later changed his enrollment to the Republican Party.{{cite web |title=Minutes of the Meeting of the State Committee, March 8, 2026 |url=https://mywikis-wiki-media.s3.us-central-1.wasabisys.com/lpedia/LPNY_MINUTES_2026-03-08_APPROVED_2026-09-27.pdf |publisher=Libertarian Party of New York |access-date=November 4, 2026}} His running mate in that effort was Lewis County Sheriff Michael Carpinelli.{{cite web |title=Mark Braiman Nominated for Lt. Governor |url=https://lpny.org/2026/03/31/mark-braiman-nominated-for-lt-governor/ |publisher=Libertarian Party of New York |date=March 31, 2026 |access-date=November 4, 2026}} Blakeman ultimately faced no contested primary. On March 8, 2026, the State Committee voted 9–12 against entering Carpinelli, who was not an LPNY member, into nomination for lieutenant governor, short of the required three-quarters vote, and instead nominated Mark Braiman. By April, Sharpe was also discussing a possible run with commentator Shannon Joy as lieutenant governor, without seeking the party's endorsement. On April 12, with petitioning about to begin and no LPNY petition available, the State Committee voted 13–9 (3 abstaining) to rescind Sharpe's nomination. Braiman withdrew, and the committee postponed nominations for statewide office indefinitely and endorsed NOTA for governor, lieutenant governor, attorney general and comptroller without objection.{{cite web |title=Minutes of the Meeting of the State Committee, April 12, 2026 |url=https://mywikis-wiki-media.s3.us-central-1.wasabisys.com/lpedia/LPNY_MINUTES_2026-04-12_APPROVED_2026-09-27.pdf |publisher=Libertarian Party of New York |access-date=November 4, 2026}} Sharpe and Joy then sought a place on the ballot as an independent ticket under the "Coalition Party" name, with a goal of gathering 50,000 signatures in five weeks.{{cite web |title=Special Campaign HQ Meeting! '''Ramaswamy:''' {{legend0|#ffb2b2|40–50%}} {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}} {{legend0|#D72F30|70–80%}} | title = [[Governor of Ohio|Governor]] | before_election = [[Mike DeWine]] | before_party = Ohio Republican Party | after_election = [[Amy Acton]] | after_party = Ohio Democratic Party }} {{ElectionsOH}} The '''2026 Ohio gubernatorial election''' was held on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Ohio]]. Former state health director [[Amy Acton]] defeated [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] entrepreneur [[Vivek Ramaswamy]]. Republican incumbent governor [[Mike DeWine]] was ineligible to seek a third consecutive term. [[Primary elections]] were held on May 5, with Ramaswamy defeating minimal opposition for the Republican nomination and Acton running unopposed for the Democratic nomination. Acton became Ohio's first elected female{{Efn|[[Nancy Hollister]] served as governor, albeit for only 11 days, following [[George Voinovich]]'s resignation to take his seat in the [[U.S. Senate]].}} and first Jewish governor.{{cite news |title=Democrat Amy Acton is Ohio's next governor, according to unofficial election results |url=https://www.news5cleveland.com/news/politics/ohio-politics/democrat-amy-acton-is-ohios-next-governor |last=Trau |first=Morgan |access-date=November 4, 2026 |publisher=News 5 Cleveland |date=November 3, 2026}} If he had been elected, Ramaswamy would have become the first [[Indian American]] governor of Ohio and the first [[Hindus|Hindu]] governor in the United States.{{Efn|[[Bobby Jindal]] was raised Hindu but converted to Christianity as a teenager.}} The campaign was described as "ugly" and heavily reliant on [[negative campaigning]]. Ramaswamy directly attacked Acton's background, questioning her mental fitness for office by making claims that the childhood abuse she faced was exaggerated. Ramaswamy also faced harsh criticism for [[2026 Ohio Ramaswamy campaign attack ad controversy|his false attack ads]] featuring Acton's estranged mother. Acton, meanwhile, labeled Ramaswamy an "out-of-touch [[Plutocracy|plutocrat]]" and "con artist."{{Cite news |last=Contrera |first=Jessica |date=October 20, 2026 |title=Attack Ad Featuring Candidate's Mother Turns Ohio Governor's Race Even Uglier |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/20/us/politics/ramaswamy-campaign-ad-acton-estranged-mother-donna-arthur.html |access-date=October 21, 2026 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} Polls throughout most of the campaign indicated a competitive race, with Acton holding a small advantage. However, following the release of the widely condemned ad of Acton's mother, Ramaswamy fell behind further in the polls, causing many news organizations to predict a Democratic flip.{{Cite web |last=Isenstadt |first=Alex |date=October 28, 2026 |title=Exclusive: Controversial ad backfiring on Ramaswamy, GOP poll finds |url=https://www.axios.com/2026/10/28/gop-poll-ramaswamy-ad-damage |access-date=November 6, 2026 |website=Axios |language=en}} These predictions were proven correct, as Acton won the election by a comfortable eight-point margin. This is the first time Democrats have won a gubernatorial election in Ohio since [[2006 Ohio gubernatorial election|2006]]. Acton will be inaugurated on January 11, 2027.{{cite web |last1=Muhammad |first1=Mariyam |title=Can Mike DeWine run for Ohio governor in 2026? What to know about term limits |url=https://www.dispatch.com/story/news/2024/11/08/mike-dewine-run-ohio-governor-2026-state-law-says/76111304007/ |website=[[The Columbus Dispatch]] Lehnerd == General election == === Campaign === On September 2, Ramaswamy accepted invitations to participate in gubernatorial debates hosted by [[CNN]] and [[WLWT]] and called on Acton to join him. Acton's campaign subsequently declined, citing what it characterized as inaccurate and personal attacks in Ramaswamy's campaign advertising. As a result, no debates between the two major-party nominees were held.{{cite web |last1=Bischoff |first1=Laura A. |title=Amy Acton refuses to debate Vivek Ramaswamy in Ohio governor's race |url=https://www.dispatch.com/story/news/state/2026/09/02/ohio-governor-candidates-may-not-debate-find-out-why/91585349007/ |website=[[The Columbus Dispatch]] |date=September 2, 2026 |access-date=September 4, 2026}} ==== Canfield Fair incident ==== On September 6, Acton was attacked at a campaign event at the [[Canfield, Ohio|Canfield]] Fair. An armed individual lunged at her and was apprehended by local authorities. Several campaign volunteers suffered minor injuries.{{Cite web |last=Knue |first=Kurt |date=September 6, 2026 |title=Amy Acton attacked at campaign event near Youngstown; multiple people reportedly injured |url=https://www.wlwt.com/article/amy-acton-attacked-at-campaign-event-near-youngstown/73625988 |access-date=September 6, 2026 |website=WLWT |language=en}} The suspect, Patrick Havas, was charged with "two counts of assault and one count of disorderly conduct."{{cite web |last1=Ziegler |first1=Jen |title=Armed man arrested after pushing toward Amy Acton is brother of Ramaswamy donor who quit Husted campaign |url=https://tiffinohio.net/posts/patrick-havas-arrested-acton-attack-brother-ramaswamy-donor/ |website=TiffinOhio.net |date=September 6, 2026 |access-date=September 25, 2026}} ==== Gas tax holiday ==== On September 21, Acton called for an emergency [[gas tax holiday]] to provide relief to Ohioans amid rising [[Gasoline and diesel usage and pricing|fuel prices]]. Ramaswamy subsequently proposed suspending Ohio's gasoline and diesel taxes for 90 days, working with Republican legislative leaders to advance the measure. On September 30, the [[Ohio General Assembly]] passed House Bill 519, which temporarily suspended the state's gasoline and diesel taxes for 90 days, with $725 million in state general revenue funds allocated to replace the lost revenue. Governor [[Mike DeWine]] signed the bill into law on October 1, with the tax holiday taking effect on October 4.{{cite web |last1=Evans |first1=Nick |title=Ohio lawmakers approve 90-day gas tax holiday just weeks ahead of election |url=https://ohiocapitaljournal.com/2026/09/30/ohio-lawmakers-approve-90-day-gas-tax-holiday-just-weeks-ahead-of-election/ |website=[[Ohio Capital Journal]] 2026}} ==== Attacks on Amy Acton's upbringing and ad controversy ==== The Ramaswamy campaign was described as "ugly" and heavily focused upon [[negative campaigning]].{{Cite news |last=Contrera |first=Jessica |date=October 20, 2026 |title=Attack Ad Featuring Candidate's Mother Turns Ohio Governor's Race Even Uglier |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/20/us/politics/ramaswamy-campaign-ad-acton-estranged-mother-donna-arthur.html |access-date=October 20, 2026 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} An [[attack ad]] by the Ramaswamy campaign focused on Acton's background to portray her as dishonest and [[Mental disorder|mentally ill]], claiming that she had "lied" and "exaggerated" about being abused, despite evidence that she had undergone [[Child sexual abuse|childhood rape]], other types of [[sexual abuse]], [[Homelessness in the United States|homelessness]], millions to promote it |url=https://apnews.com/article/election-2026-ohio-governor-acton-mother-ramaswamy-dc59bd5f0c47f9e06f37022e2ba2cce5 |access-date=October 21, 2026 |website=[[Associated Press]]}}{{Cite web |date=October 20, 2026 |title=Amy Acton's Mom Claims Candidate Lied About Childhood in Attack Ad — Despite Extensive Record of Abuse |url=https://www.nationalreview.com/news/amy-actons-mom-claims-candidate-lied-about-childhood-in-attack-ad-despite-extensive-record-of-abuse/ |access-date=October 20, 2026 |website=National Review |language=en-US}}{{Cite news |last=Tumulty |first=Karen |date=October 20, 2026 |title=Ohio governor's race in uproar over video featuring Democrat's estranged mother |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/10/20/ohio-governors-race-uproar-over-video-featuring-democrats-estranged-mother/ |access-date=October 21, 2026 |newspaper=The Washington Post |language=en-US |issn=0190-8286}} The ad – which featured Acton's mother, Donna Arthur, denouncing her – received nationwide attention after it was publicized on social media on October 19. Acton has been estranged from Arthur since she was [[Child protective services|removed]] from the family home at the age of 12 after her stepfather was charged with raping her. Acton's brother said the two were removed from their mother's custody after their stepfather was indicted for raping Acton as a child. Acton has not seen Arthur since. Her mother's husband was indicted but failed to reappear for trial and has since died. The advertisement was first publicized by Ohio political blogger D.J. Byrnes, who writes under the pseudonym ''The Rooster''. Byrnes had learned that the campaign was developing an advertisement featuring Acton's mother and subsequently obtained a recording of it through a political message-testing survey conducted by the polling firm [[Dynata]].{{cite web |last1=Pelzer|first1=Jeremy|title=How a provocative blogger was first to reveal Vivek's Ramaswamy explosive attack ad|url=https://www.cleveland.com/news/2026/10/how-a-provocative-blogger-was-first-to-reveal-viveks-ramaswamy-explosive-attack-ad.html|website=[[The Plain Dealer]]|date=October 26, 2026|access-date=November 6, 2026}} Connie Luck, a spokesperson for Ramaswamy's campaign, took credit for creating it and said the ad will "air both online and on TV in the closing days of the campaign". '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#D2B1D9|40–50%}} {{legend0|#AE8BB1|50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No votes}} }} {{ElectionsOK}} The '''2026 Oklahoma gubernatorial election''' took place on November 3, 2026, to elect the next [[governor of Oklahoma]]. [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] former state senator [[Mike Mazzei]] and [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] state representative [[Cyndi Munson]] were the nominees for their respective parties. Republican incumbent [[Kevin Stitt]] was [[Term limits in the United States|term-limited]] and ineligible to seek a third term. Primary elections were held on June 16, 2026, and in races where no candidate receives over 50% of the vote, runoff elections took place on August 25, 2026. Mike Mazzei won the general election by about 6%. This was the best performance for a Democrat in a gubernatorial election in Oklahoma since [[2006 Oklahoma gubernatorial election|2006]], which was the last time a Democrat won, and the closest election since [[2002 Oklahoma gubernatorial election|2002]]. ==Republican primary== ===Campaign=== In August 2023, [[KOSU]] noted that Attorney General [[Gentner Drummond]] had raised significantly more than other statewide elected officials in 2023, fueling rumors of a gubernatorial run.{{cite news |last1=Nissley |first1=Isabel |title=Oklahoma Attorney General raises $225K, topping state officials' campaign contributions |url=https://www.kosu.org/politics/2023-08-08/oklahoma-attorney-general-raises-225k-topping-state-officials-campaign-contributions |access-date=25 August 2023 |work=[[KOSU]] |date=August 8, 2023}} The same month, ''[[The Black Wall Street Times]]'' reported State Superintendent of Public Instruction [[Ryan Walters (American politician)|Ryan Walters]] was preparing for a 2026 gubernatorial campaign.{{cite news |title=Sources: Ryan Walters mulls bid for governor amid attacks on TPS |url=https://theblackwallsttimes.com/2023/08/07/sources-ryan-walters-mulls-bid-for-governor-amid-attacks-on-tps/ |access-date=25 August 2023 |work=[[The Black Wall Street Times]] |date=August 7, 2023}} U.S. Representative [[Kevin Hern]] was the first major contender to public acknowledge he was considering a campaign in August 2024, but ruled out a run that December after House Republicans won a narrow majority in the [[2024 United States House of Representatives elections|2024 elections]].{{cite news |last1=Krehbiel |first1=Randy |title=Could Congressman Kevin Hern be Oklahoma's next governor? |url=https://tulsaworld.com/news/state-regional/government-politics/could-congressman-kevin-hern-be-oklahomas-next-governor/article_dfbf99fe-6585-11ef-a997-3319440d32fb.html |access-date=August 30, 2024 |work=[[Tulsa World]] |date=August 29, 2024 |language=en}} In early January 2025, former state senator [[Mike Mazzei]] posted a gubernatorial campaign logo to [[Facebook]].{{Cite news |first1= Reese |last1=Gorman |last2=Luetkemeyer |first2=Em |date=January 12, 2025 |title=Oklahoma Attorney General Prepares to Jump in Governor's Race |url=https://www.notus.org/oklahoma/oklahoma-attorney-general-prepares-governor-race |access-date=January 12, 2025 |work=NOTUS |language=en-US}} On January 13, 2025, Drummond announced his campaign for governor. He was the first major candidate to enter the race and the second overall after Leisa Mitchell Haynes. On February 18, former Oklahoma House Speaker [[Charles McCall]] officially announced his campaign. Mazzei officially launched his campaign on April 3. In May, former state senator [[Jake A. Merrick|Jake Merrick]] entered the race followed by businessman Kenneth Sturgell.
