'''Kotek:''' {{legend0|#A5B0FF|40–50%}} {{legend0|#7996E2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674DE|60–70%}} {{legend0|#584CDE|70–80%}}
'''Drazan:''' {{legend0|#E27F7F|50–60%}} {{legend0|#D75D5D|60–70%}} {{legend0|#D72F30|70–80%}} {{legend0|#C21B18|80–90%}} }} {{ElectionsOR}} The '''2026 Oregon gubernatorial election''' was held on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Oregon]]. [[Democratic Party of Oregon|Democratic]] incumbent [[Tina Kotek]] sought a second term, and was challenged by 2022 [[Oregon Republican Party|Republican]] gubernatorial nominee [[Christine Drazan]]. This election marked Oregon's first gubernatorial rematch since [[1978 Oregon gubernatorial election|1978]]. [[Primary elections]] took place on May 19, 2026.{{Cite web|date=May 9, 2025 |title=2026 State Primary Election Dates|url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|website=[[National Conference of State Legislatures]]|access-date=August 5, 2025}} Kotek won the Democratic nomination with 84% of the vote, while Drazan won the Republican nomination with 41% of the vote.{{cite web |title=Oregon Governor Election Results |url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/11/03/us/elections/results-oregon-governor.html |website=The New York Times |publisher=The New York Times |access-date=November 4, 2026}} Kotek won re-election by just under 10 points, according to unofficial results. Besides improving on her numbers in the counties she carried in 2022, Kotek flipped [[Clackamas County, Oregon|Clackamas]] and [[Deschutes County, Oregon|Deschutes]] counties to the Democratic column. While ultimately losing them, she came within five points of Drazan in [[Marion County, Oregon|Marion County]], and within ten points in [[Jackson County, Oregon|Jackson]] and [[Tillamook County, Oregon|Tillamook]] counties. While Democrats have won every gubernatorial election in Oregon since [[1982 Oregon gubernatorial election|1982]], only one of these victories, in [[1998 Oregon gubernatorial election|1998]], has been by a margin greater than 10 points.{{Cite web |last=Mason |first=Anastasia |title=Blue wave lifted Gov. Tina Kotek, but her margins tell a deeper story |url=https://www.statesmanjournal.com/story/news/politics/elections/2026/11/10/oregon-gov-tina-kotek-results-by-county/92700080007/ |access-date=November 11, 2026 |website=Statesman Journal |language=en-US}} Kotek became the first Oregon gubernatorial candidate to receive over a million votes. '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#D2B1D9|40–50%}} {{legend0|#AE8BB1|50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No votes}} }}{{Elections in Pennsylvania sidebar}} The '''2026 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election''' was held on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Pennsylvania]]. [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] incumbent [[Josh Shapiro]] won a second term, defeating [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] state treasurer [[Stacy Garrity]] in a landslide. [[Primary elections]] were held on May 19, 2026.{{Cite web|date=September 26, 2025|title=2026 State Primary Election Dates|url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260509222424/https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|archive-date=May 9, 2026|access-date=September 27, 2025|website=[[National Conference of State Legislatures]]}} Shapiro and Garrity secured their nominations unopposed. This was one of five Democratic-held governorships up for election in 2026 in a state that [[Donald Trump]] won in the [[2024 United States presidential election|2024 presidential election]]. Although Pennsylvania is one of the nation's most premier swing states at the federal level, the gubernatorial election was never considered in serious contention. Josh Shapiro won the governor's mansion by a very comfortable margin [[2022 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election|four years earlier]], and was widely expected to repeat that performance in 2026. Polls consistently showed him leading by 20 points or more against his Republican challenger, which was reflected in the final results on election night. Shapiro became the first gubernatorial candidate to win 60 percent of the vote since [[Ed Rendell]] in [[2006 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election|2006]]. == Background == [[Pennsylvania]] is a [[purple state]] located in the [[Northeastern United States]]. A part of the [[Rust Belt]], it was narrowly won by Republican [[Donald Trump]] in [[2024 United States presidential election in Pennsylvania|his non-consecutive second victory in 2024]] after similarly narrow victories by Democrat [[Joe Biden]] in [[2020 United States presidential election in Pennsylvania|2020]] and Trump in his first election in [[2016 United States presidential election in Pennsylvania|2016]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/revisit-pennsylvania-election-results/|title=Revisit Pennsylvania election results from 2020 and 2016 ahead of Election Day 2024 - CBS News|date=November 4, 2024|website=www.cbsnews.com}}{{Cite web |title=The 2024 presidential election was close, not a landslide |url=https://abcnews.com/538/2024-presidential-election-close-landslide/story?id=116240898 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241126224157/https://abcnews.go.com/538/2024-presidential-election-close-landslide/story?id=116240898 |url-status=live |archive-date=November 26, 2024 |website=ABC News}} The state has a Democratic and Republican senator, making it one of only three states to have a split Senate delegation,{{efn|The other two are [[Maine]], with an independent who caucuses with the Democrats and a Republican, and [[Wisconsin]], with a Democrat and a Republican.[https://smartpolitics.lib.umn.edu/2024/11/19/119th-congress-smashes-record-low-for-number-of-split-us-senate-delegations/ 119th Congress Smashes Record Low for Number of Split US Senate Delegations], Smart Politics, November 19, 2024. Retrieved January 31, 2026}} while Republicans hold a majority in the state's House delegation, with ten seats to the Democrats' seven.{{cite news |title=119th Congress Smashes Record Low for Number of Split US Senate Delegations |url=https://smartpolitics.lib.umn.edu/2024/11/19/119th-congress-smashes-record-low-for-number-of-split-us-senate-delegations/ |access-date=September 4, 2025 |issue=Smart Politics |date=November 19, 2024}} Democrats also control the [[Pennsylvania House of Representatives]] while Republicans control the [[Pennsylvania Senate]].{{cite news |title=Democrats will again control Pennsylvania House after holding on to one-seat majority |url=https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2024/11/pennsylvania-election-results-2024-state-house-democratic-republican-control/ |access-date=September 4, 2025 |publisher=Spotlight PA |date=November 8, 2024}} Republicans have not won a Pennsylvania gubernatorial election since [[2010 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election|2010]]. '''Block''': {{legend0|#D9D9D9|30–40%}} {{legend0|#BDBDBD|40–50%}} | election_date = November 3, 2026 | title = [[Governor of Rhode Island|Governor]] | before_election = [[Dan McKee]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Helena Foulkes]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsRI}} The '''2026 Rhode Island gubernatorial election''' was held on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Rhode Island]]. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[Dan McKee]] ran for re-election to a second full term but was defeated in the primary by [[Helena Buonanno Foulkes|Helena Foulkes]]. [[Primary elections]] took place on September 9, 2026.{{Cite web|date=September 26, 2025|title=2026 State Primary Election Dates|url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260509222424/https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|archive-date=May 9, 2026|url-status=live|access-date=September 27, 2025|website=[[National Conference of State Legislatures]]}} Republicans have not won a statewide election in Rhode Island since [[2006 Rhode Island gubernatorial election|2006]]. While Rhode Island is generally a safely Democratic state, the Democratic primary was predicted to be competitive due to McKee's high unpopularity. The election has also been noted as not following national trends of progressives versus moderates, with both Democrats being relatively moderate and the primary instead largely boiling down to anger over the longtime closure of the [[Washington Bridge (Providence, Rhode Island)|Washington Bridge]].{{Cite web |last1=Okun |first1=Eli |date=August 8, 2026 |title=Why Rhode Island may oust a sitting governor over a bridge |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2026/08/08/rhode-island-governor-bridge-01030024 |access-date=2026-08-12 |website=Politico |language=en}} This is the first election since [[2014 Hawaii gubernatorial election|2014]] in which an elected state governor lost renomination.{{efn|Governor [[Jeff Colyer]] of Kansas, who had taken office after the resignation of [[Sam Brownback]], was defeated by [[Kris Kobach]] in the [[2018 Kansas gubernatorial election|2018]] Republican primary election.}} It is also the first time since [[1994 Rhode Island gubernatorial election|1994]] in which an incumbent governor of Rhode Island lost renomination. ==Democratic primary== ===Candidates=== ====Nominee==== *[[Helena Foulkes]], former [[CVS Pharmacy|CVS]] executive, granddaughter of former U.S. senator [[Thomas J. '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#d2b1d9|40–50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No votes}} | title = [[Governor of South Carolina|Governor]] | before_election = [[Henry McMaster]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Alan Wilson (politician)|Alan Wilson]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) | last_update = November 11, 2026, 12:21 AM ET }} {{ElectionsSC}} The '''2026 South Carolina gubernatorial election''' was held on November 3, 2026, to elect the next [[governor of South Carolina]]. [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] state attorney general [[Alan Wilson (politician)|Alan Wilson]] defeated [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] state representative [[Jermaine Johnson (politician)|Jermaine Johnson]] in the general election.{{Cite news |last=Walker |first=Abigail |date=2026-11-03 |title=Alan Wilson wins South Carolina governor’s race |url=https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/6185074-alan-wilson-wins-south-carolina-governors-race-2026/ |access-date=2026-11-08 |work=The Hill |language=en-US}} Republican incumbent [[Henry McMaster]] was ineligible to seek a third consecutive term. In the Republican primary on June 9, Lieutenant Governor [[Pamela Evette]] emerged as the top vote-getter with the help of an endorsement from President [[Donald Trump]], but did not secure a majority needed to win the nomination, triggering a June 23 runoff between her and Wilson. After Trump announced his support for both Wilson and Evette, Wilson was nominated in the runoff with 68.6% of the vote. Johnson won the Democratic nomination in the June 9 primary with 59.7% of the vote against Billy Webster, the chief of staff for former governor [[Richard Riley]]. Democrats have not won a gubernatorial election in South Carolina since [[1998 South Carolina gubernatorial election|1998]].{{Cite web |last=Holdman |first=Jessica |date=October 28, 2025 |title=SC Democratic Rep. Jermaine Johnson announces campaign for governor |url=https://scdailygazette.com/2025/10/28/sc-democratic-rep-jermaine-johnson-announces-campaign-for-governor/ |access-date=June 16, 2026 |website=SC Daily Gazette |language=en-US}} This was the closest South Carolina gubernatorial election since [[1994 South Carolina gubernatorial election|1994]]. ==Republican primary== [[File:Pamela Evette 2019.jpg|thumb|x170px|[[Lieutenant Governor of South Carolina]] [[Pamela Evette]], who was defeated in the Republican primary runoff.]] [[File:Ralph Norman official photo (cropped 3).jpg|thumb|x170px|[[U.S. Representative]] [[Ralph Norman]], who finished third in the Republican primary.]] [[File:Nancy Mace.jpg|thumb|x170px|[[U.S. Representative]] [[Nancy Mace]], who finished fifth in the Republican primary.]] ===Candidates=== ====Nominee==== *[[Alan Wilson (politician)|Alan Wilson]], [[attorney general of South Carolina]] (2011–present){{cite news |last1=Kinnard |first1=Meg |title=Alan Wilson, South Carolina's four-term Republican attorney general, enters 2026 governor's race |url=https://www.wyff4.com/article/alan-wilson-south-carolina-attorney-general-enters-2026-governors-race/65162744 |access-date=June 23, 2025 |work=[[Associated Press]] |date=June 23, 2025 |language=en}} ** Running mate: [[Mike Reichenbach (politician)|Mike Reichenbach]], [[South Carolina Senate|state senator]] from the 31st district (2022–present){{cite web |last1=Renaud |first1=Tim |title=Wilson taps SC Sen. '''Ahlers:''' {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674de|60–70%}} {{legend0|#584cde|70–80%}} {{legend0|#3933e5|80–90%}} | title = [[Governor of South Dakota|Governor]] | before_election = [[Larry Rhoden]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Larry Rhoden]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsSD}} The '''2026 South Dakota gubernatorial election''' took place on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of South Dakota]]. The primary elections were held on June 2, 2026, and since no candidate received over 35% in the Republican primary, a runoff election was held on July 28.{{Cite web |title=South Dakota 2026 General Election |url=https://www.thegreenpapers.com/G26/SD |access-date=2025-06-13 |website=The Green Papers}} Incumbent Republican [[Larry Rhoden]], who ascended to the office of governor in 2025 after [[Kristi Noem]] resigned to become [[U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security|secretary of homeland security]], won his first full term in office. Rhoden had previously been serving as lieutenant governor under Noem since the two took office in 2019. '''Blackburn:''' {{legend0|#ffb2b2|40–50%}} {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}} {{legend0|#d72f30|70–80%}}
'''Green:''' {{legend0|#A5B0FF|40–50%}} {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674de|60–70%}} {{legend0|#584cde|70–80%}} | title = [[Governor of Tennessee|Governor]] | before_election = [[Bill Lee (Tennessee politician)|Bill Lee]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Marsha Blackburn]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsTN}} The '''2026 Tennessee gubernatorial election''' was held on November 3, 2026 to elect the [[governor of Tennessee]] for a four-year term starting on January 16, 2027. Incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] governor [[Bill Lee (Tennessee politician)|Bill Lee]] was [[Term limits in the United States|term-limited]] and ineligible to seek a third consecutive term. Republican U.S. senator [[Marsha Blackburn]] narrowly defeated [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] [[Memphis City Council|Memphis City Council member]] Jerri Green.{{Cite news |last=Browning |first=Kellen |last2=Zhang |first2=Christine |last3=Wagner |first3=Bayliss |last4=Reynolds |first4=Evan |last5=Medina |first5=Jennifer |last6=Hubler |first6=Shawn |last7=Schleifer |first7=Theodore |last8=Reynolds |first8=Evan |last9=Spoto |first9=Maia |date=2026-11-03 |title=Tennessee Governor 2026: Live Election Results, Green vs. Blackburn |url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/11/03/us/elections/results-tennessee-governor.html |access-date=2026-11-04 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} Blackburn received 45.5% of the vote to Green's 43.0%, winning by approximately 54,000 votes. The [[primary elections]] took place on August 6, 2026, with Blackburn and Green securing the Republican and Democratic nominations, respectively.{{Cite web|date=May 9, 2025 |title=2026 State Primary Election Dates |url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|website= NCSL |access-date=5 August 2025}} Blackburn significantly underperformed compared to previous Republican gubernatorial candidates. In [[2022 Tennessee gubernatorial election|2022]], Bill Lee won re-election by 32 percentage points, while Blackburn won by just 2.5 points. All 95 counties shifted toward Democrats, with [[Knox County, Tennessee|Knox]], [[Hamilton County, Tennessee|Hamilton]], [[Haywood County, Tennessee|Haywood]], [[Madison County, Tennessee|Madison]], [[Montgomery County, Tennessee|Montgomery]], and [[Rutherford County, Tennessee|Rutherford]] counties flipping Democratic.{{Cite web |last=Maynard |first=Chasity |last2=Brown |first2=Kassidy |date=2026-11-09 |title=Democrats flipped 5 Tennessee counties in the 2026 midterms. See how your county voted |url=https://www.wsmv.com/2026/11/09/democrats-flipped-5-tennessee-counties-2026-midterms-see-how-your-county-voted/ |access-date=2026-11-09 |website=wsmv.com |language=en}}{{Cite news |date=2026-11-03 |title=2026 Tennessee Governor Live Election Results |url=https://votes.decisiondeskhq.com/races/2026-11-03/tennessee-governor-general-election |access-date=2026-11-07 |work=Decision Desk HQ Votes |language=en}} [[Independent politician|Independent]] candidate David Hatley also attracted support from conservative voters dissatisfied with Blackburn, receiving 9.3% of the statewide vote, or nearly 196,000 votes, and finishing third.{{Cite web |last=Smith |first=Chris |date=2026-11-05 |title=Trump voters stayed home, Montgomery County swings blue: 4 takeaways on election {{!}} ANALYSIS - ClarksvilleNow.com |url=https://clarksvillenow.com/local/trump-voters-stayed-home-montgomery-county-swings-blue-4-takeaways-on-election-analysis/ |access-date=2026-11-07 |language=en-US}}{{Cite web |last=Motycka |first=Eli |date=2026-11-02 |title=Disaffected conservatives flock to independent David Hatley |url=https://www.nashvillepost.com/politics/state/david-hatley-conservative-voters-tennessee-governor/article_216c3a47-6c2e-5a0f-adb0-98981d1ad5fb.html |access-date=2026-11-07 |website=Nashville Post |language=en}} This was the closest Tennessee gubernatorial election since [[1896 Tennessee gubernatorial election|1896]]. Blackburn became the first woman elected governor of Tennessee and the first candidate since [[1932 Tennessee gubernatorial election|1932]] to win the governorship with less than 50% of the popular vote, securing the smallest margin of victory in a Tennessee gubernatorial election in more than a century. She will take office in January 2027.{{Cite web |date=2026-11-04 |title=Sen. Marsha Blackburn elected Tennessee governor. What’s next for schools? |url=https://www.chalkbeat.org/tennessee/2026/11/04/marsha-blackburn-elected-governor-education-policy/ |access-date=2026-11-11 |website=Chalkbeat |language=en}} Her victory extended Republican control of the governorship, which the party has held since 2011.{{Cite web |last=Jarrett |first=Kim |date=2026-08-06 |title=Tennessee poised to have its first female governor |url=https://www.themountaineer.com/news/national/tennessee-poised-to-have-its-first-female-governor/article_a34121c2-26dc-503a-8fac-d4ae12051c66.html |access-date=2026-08-13 |website=The Mountaineer |language=en}} {{toclimit|2}} ==Republican primary== === Candidates === ====Nominee==== *[[Marsha Blackburn]], U.S. senator (2019–present){{cite news |last1=Taylor |first1=Sarah Grace |title=Marsha Blackburn announces run for Governor of Tennessee |url=https://nashvillebanner.com/2025/08/06/marsha-blackburn-tennessee-governor-campaign-launch/ |access-date=August 6, 2025 |work=[[Nashville Banner]] |date=August 6, 2025}} ====Eliminated in primary==== *[[Monty Fritts]], [[Tennessee House of Representatives|state representative]] from the 32nd district (2023–present){{cite news |last1=Grace Taylor |first1=Sarah |title=State Rep. '''Abbott:''' {{legend0|#ffb2b2|40–50%}} {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}} {{legend0|#d72f30|70–80%}} {{legend0|#C21B18|80–90%}} {{legend0|#A80000|>90%}} }} {{ElectionsTX}} The '''2026 Texas gubernatorial election''' took place on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Texas]]. [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] state representative [[Gina Hinojosa]] defeated [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] incumbent [[Greg Abbott]], who was seeking a record fourth term,{{cite web |url= https://www.texastribune.org/2025/11/09/texas-greg-abbott-reelection-campaign-governor/ |title=Gov. Greg Abbott launches reelection campaign for fourth term |date=November 9, 2025 |access-date=November 9, 2025 |publisher= |last=Gou |first=Kayla|website=[[The Texas Tribune]]}} in an [[upset victory]]. [[Primary elections]] were held on March 3, 2026. Facing minimal opposition, Abbott won the Republican nomination with 82% of the vote. Hinojosa won the Democratic nomination with 59% of the vote over a field of candidates that included former congressman [[Chris Bell (politician)|Chris Bell]]. Hinojosa's win was part of a broad wave of victories for Democrats in Texas, who flipped every statewide office on the ballot from Republican control. Hinojosa is the first Democrat to win a gubernatorial election in Texas since [[Ann Richards]] in [[1990 Texas gubernatorial election|1990]],{{Cite web |last=Mendoza |first=Madalyn |date=November 4, 2026 |title=Hinojosa defeats Abbott, flips Texas governor's office blue |url=https://www.axios.com/local/san-antonio/2026/11/04/texas-governor-race-results-hinojosa-abbott |access-date=November 4, 2026 |website=[[Axios (website)|Axios]] |language=en}}{{Cite web |date=November 4, 2026 |title=Texas Governor Election 2026 Live Results: Gina Hinojosa Wins |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-elections/texas-governor-results |access-date=November 4, 2026 |website=[[NBC News]] |language=en}} while Abbott is the first incumbent governor of Texas to lose reelection since Richards' reelection bid in [[1994 Texas gubernatorial election|1994]].{{cite web |last1=Guo |first1=Kayla |title=Democrat Gina Hinojosa topples Greg Abbott to become first Latina governor of Texas |url=https://www.texastribune.org/2026/11/03/texas-governor-greg-abbott-gina-hinojosa-election/ |website=[[The Texas Tribune]] |access-date=November 6, 2026|date=November 3, 2026|first3=Terri|last3=Langford|first2=Taylor|last2=Goldenstein}} Additionally, Hinojosa won the largest margin for a Democrat in the state since [[1982 Texas gubernatorial election|1982]]. In contrast, with his term scheduled to end on January 19, 2027,{{cite news |url=https://www.tpr.org/government-politics/2026-11-11/when-will-incoming-texas-gov-gina-hinojosa-take-office |title=When will incoming Texas Gov. Gina Hinojosa take office? |publisher=Texas Public Radio |last=Drusch |first=Andrea |date=November 11, 2026 |accessdate=November 11, 2026}} Abbott is the [[List of longest-serving United States governors|longest-serving incumbent governor]] to be defeated for reelection since [[Mario Cuomo]] in [[1994 New York gubernatorial election|1994]]. {{toclimit|3}} ==Republican primary== ===Candidates=== ====Nominee==== * [[Greg Abbott]], incumbent [[Governor of Texas|governor]] (2015–present) ====Eliminated in primary==== * R.F. '''Janoo:''' {{legend0|#a5b0ff|40–50%}} {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} | title = [[Governor of Vermont|Governor]] | before_election = [[Phil Scott]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Phil Scott]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{Elections in Vermont}} The '''2026 Vermont gubernatorial election''' was held on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Vermont]]. [[Vermont Republican Party|Republican]] incumbent [[Phil Scott]] was re-elected to a sixth two-year term. He defeated [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] economist Amanda Janoo by a much narrower margin than his previous landslide reelections. [[Primary elections]] were held on August 11, 2026.{{Cite web|date=May 9, 2025|title=2026 State Primary Election Dates|url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260523194629/https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|archive-date=May 23, 2026|website=[[National Conference of State Legislatures]]|access-date=5 August 2025}} Along with neighboring [[2026 New Hampshire gubernatorial election|New Hampshire]], this is one of two Republican-held governorships up for election in a state that [[Kamala Harris]] won in the [[2024 United States presidential election|2024 presidential election]], and the only Republican-held governorship in a state that Harris won by a double-digit margin. With the defeat of Governor [[Greg Abbott]] in [[2026 Texas gubernatorial election|Texas]], Scott will become the longest serving incumbent Governor in the United States in 2027. This was also the first gubernatorial election since [[2018 Vermont gubernatorial election|2018]] where the Democratic candidate won any counties in the state. Provided Scott completes his sixth term, he will become the longest serving [[List of governors of Vermont|Governor of Vermont]] in state history surpassing the previous record set by [[Howard Dean]]. == Background == In November 2024, Governor [[Phil Scott]] won re-election in a landslide, and Vermont Republicans were able to break Democratic supermajorities in the [[Vermont Senate]] and [[Vermont General Assembly]], and flip the office of [[Lieutenant Governor of Vermont|lieutenant governor]][https://www.governing.com/politics/the-blue-state-where-republicans-scored-their-biggest-gains The Blue State Where Republicans Scored Their Biggest Gains], Governing, November 14, 2024{{Cite web|url=https://vtdigger.org/2025/01/09/republican-john-rodgers-formally-elected-vermonts-next-lieutenant-governor/|title=Republican John Rodgers formally elected Vermont’s next lieutenant governor|first=Shaun|last=Robinson|date=January 9, 2025}} despite Vermont's deeply blue partisan lean at the federal and state levels.{{Cite web|url=https://www.geocurrents.info/blog/2022/12/09/the-vermont-paradox-a-left-wing-state-with-a-remarkably-popular-republican-governor/|title=The Vermont Paradox: A Left-Wing State with a Remarkably Popular Republican Governor|first=Martin W.|last=Lewis|date=December 9, 2022}} According to the polling company [[Morning Consult]], Scott had been the most popular state governor in the entire nation.{{Cite web |title=U.S. Governor Approval Rating Tracker |url=https://pro.morningconsult.com/trackers/governor-approval-ratings |access-date=2025-07-18 |website=Morning Consult Pro |language=en}} Before this cycle, he had won re-election four times by increasingly wider margins since he was first elected in [[2016 Vermont gubernatorial election|2016]].{{Cite news |last=Kinzel |first=Bob |date=2022-08-10 |title=It's primary day in Vermont. 2026 Wisconsin gubernatorial election.text:

'''Tiffany:''' {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}} {{legend0|#d72f30|70–80%}} | title = [[Governor of Wisconsin|Governor]] | before_election = [[Tony Evers]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[David Crowley]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsWI}} The '''2026 Wisconsin gubernatorial election''' was held on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Wisconsin]]. The [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] nominee, Milwaukee County executive [[David Crowley]], was elected governor, defeating [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] U.S. representative [[Tom Tiffany]]. When sworn in in January 2027, Crowley will become the first African-American governor of Wisconsin and the fifth African-American governor in U.S. history.{{Cite web |last=Gilbert |first=Craig |title=Gilbert: How small voting shifts made Wisconsin the closest state in the nation |url=https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/politics/elections/2024/11/25/gilbert-small-voting-shifts-made-wisconsin-2024s-closest-state/76461074007/ |website=[[Milwaukee Journal Sentinel]] |language=en-US |date=November 25, 2024 |access-date=November 26, 2024}} Incumbent Democratic governor [[Tony Evers]] did not seek re-election to a third term, making this the first open-seat gubernatorial election in Wisconsin since [[2010 Wisconsin gubernatorial election|2010]].{{Cite web |last=Beck |first=Molly |title=Wisconsin's Democratic Gov. Tony Evers won't seek a third term in 2026 |url=https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/politics/2025/07/24/wisconsin-democratic-gov-tony-evers-wont-seek-re-election-in-2026/84246291007/ |access-date=February 4, 2026 |website=Journal Sentinel |language=en-US}} Crowley's victory represents the first time since [[1962 Wisconsin gubernatorial election|1962]] that Democrats have won a third consecutive gubernatorial election in Wisconsin. [[Primary elections]] were held on August 11, 2026. Tiffany won the Republican nomination without serious challenge. Crowley, despite having temporarily withdrawn his candidacy, won the Democratic nomination in an [[upset victory]] over state representative [[Francesca Hong]], receiving 39.8% of the vote.{{Cite web |last=Mueller |first=Julia |title=Crowley defeats democratic socialist Hong to face Tiffany in Wisconsin governor's race |url=https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/6023019-crowley-wins-wisconsin-governor-primary/ |access-date=August 12, 2026 |website=The Hill |date=August 12, 2026 |language=en-US}} Crowley's victory was part of a national Democratic wave in the [[2026 United States elections|2026 elections]], which also saw [[Democratic Party of Wisconsin|Wisconsin Democrats]] gain control of the [[Wisconsin Senate|state Senate]] and [[Wisconsin State Assembly|Assembly]], achieving their first governing trifecta since [[99th Wisconsin Legislature|2009–2010]]. Crowley's margin of victory—just over eight percentage points—is the largest margin of victory in a Wisconsin gubernatorial election since [[Tommy Thompson]]'s third re-election in [[1998 Wisconsin gubernatorial election|1998]], and the largest margin for a Democrat since Thompson's predecessor, [[Tony Earl]], won election with 57% of the vote in [[1982 Wisconsin gubernatorial election|1982]]. Crowley's running mate on the Democratic ticket was [[Sarah Godlewski]], the incumbent secretary of state and former state treasurer; she was unopposed in the lieutenant gubernatorial primary. Tiffany's running mate was David Varnam, the former mayor of [[Lancaster, Wisconsin]]; the Republican Party of Wisconsin had endorsed and supported Will Martin in the lieutenant gubernatorial primary, but Varnam won the nomination in an upset. {{toclimit|4}} == Background == Wisconsin is considered to be a [[purple state]] at the federal and state levels with a uniquely competitive track record (presidential races decided by less than a point in [[2016 United States presidential election in Wisconsin|2016]], [[2020 United States presidential election in Wisconsin|2020]], and [[2024 United States presidential election in Wisconsin|2024]]; Senate races decided by roughly a point in [[2022 United States Senate election in Wisconsin|2022]] and [[2024 United States Senate election in Wisconsin|2024]]; and a governor's race decided by a point in [[2018 Wisconsin gubernatorial election|2018]]). The past two federal election cycles in Wisconsin featured split outcomes, with Democrats winning for governor and Republicans for Senate in [[2022 Wisconsin elections|2022]] and Democrats winning for Senate and Republicans for president in [[2024 Wisconsin elections|2024]]. Wisconsin has voted with the winner of the last five presidential elections, and in 2024 it had the second-highest voter turnout in the country (behind [[Minnesota]]) and one of the biggest turnout increases in the country. Both parties have seen success in the state in recent years. Republicans narrowly control both chambers of the [[Wisconsin Legislature]] and hold a majority in Wisconsin's [[United States House of Representatives|U.S. House]] delegation. However, Democrats control most statewide executive offices and have won the last two gubernatorial races.{{Cite web |last=Unger |first=Nancy C. |title=How Wisconsin Became the Ultimate Purple State |url=https://time.com/7093734/wisconsin-purple-state-history/ |website=[[TIME Magazine]] |language=en |date=October 28, 2024 |access-date=May 28, 2025}} Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[Tony Evers]] was first elected in [[2018 Wisconsin gubernatorial election|2018]], narrowly defeating incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] [[Scott Walker (politician)|Scott Walker]].{{Cite news |last=Gowen |first=Annie |title=How the Democrats finally defeated Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/how-the-democrats-finally-defeated-wisconsin-gov-scott-walker/2018/11/07/3377ed17-9cbe-4537-8b2a-acd0c37a8d35_story.html |url-access=registration |date=November 7, 2018 |access-date=May 28, 2025 |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |language=en-US |issn=0190-8286}} He was re-elected by a slightly larger margin in [[2022 Wisconsin gubernatorial election|2022]], defeating Republican businessman Tim Michels.{{Cite news |last=Bosman |first=Julie |date=November 9, 2022 |title=Tony Evers and Ron Johnson Keep Their Seats in Wisconsin |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/11/09/us/politics/wisconsin-tony-evers-ron-johnson.html |access-date=May 28, 2025 |work=[[The New York Times]] |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} In July 2025, Evers announced he would not seek re-election to a third term. The race is widely seen as a tossup due to Evers's retirement and the state's even partisan lean.{{Cite web |last=Cavalli |first=Samantha |date=July 25, 2025 |title=Political analysts call governor's seat 'a toss-up' after Evers decides to not run for a 3rd term |url=https://www.wbay.com/2025/07/25/political-analysts-call-governors-seat-toss-up-after-evers-decides-not-run-3rd-term/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250730005208/https://www.wbay.com/2025/07/25/political-analysts-call-governors-seat-toss-up-after-evers-decides-not-run-3rd-term/ |archive-date=July 30, 2025 |access-date=March 5, 2026 |website=WBAY.com}} ==Democratic primary== === Governor === Tony Evers's decision not to seek re-election triggered a competitive Democratic primary. The Associated Press described the process leading up to the August 11 primary as chaotic.{{cite web | title=Wisconsin's 2026 primary election arrives with high-profile races for governor, two congressional seats | url=https://pbswisconsin.org/news-item/wisconsins-2026-primary-election-arrives-with-high-profile-races-for-governor-two-congressional-seats/ }} Lieutenant Governor Sara Rodriguez amassed support as a centrist candidate until she dropped out in mid-July, prompting Milwaukee County executive David Crowley to re-enter the race ten days after withdrawing. The race became a showdown between Crowley, who was endorsed by Evers and other establishment figures, and state representative Francesca Hong, a [[democratic socialist]]. Crowley narrowly won the Democratic nomination in an [[upset victory]] over Hong, as polls showed him trailing Hong by nearly 20 points just a week earlier.{{Cite news |last1=Wagner |first1=Bayliss [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] state senator [[Eric Barlow]] defeated [[Constitution Party (United States)|Constitution]] nominee Rebecca Bextel and [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] perennial candidate Kenneth Casner with 68.1% of the vote. Republican incumbent [[Mark Gordon]] was [[Term limits in the United States|term-limited]] and thus ineligible to seek a third consecutive term. [[Primary elections]] took place on August 18, 2026.{{Cite web|title=2026 State Primary Election Dates|url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|website=[[National Conference of State Legislatures]]|date=May 9, 2025|access-date=August 5, 2025}} Barlow defeated state superintendent [[Megan Degenfelder]] in the Republican primary with 45.1% of the vote.{{Cite web|last=Howard|first=Andrew|date=August 18, 2026|title=Trump’s pick for Wyoming governor is the latest endorsee to lose primary|url=https://www.politico.com/news/2026/08/18/trumps-pick-for-wyoming-governor-is-the-latest-endorsee-to-lose-primary-01041404|work=[[Politico]]|access-date=August 21, 2026}} Casner secured the Democratic nomination unopposed. Democrats have not won a statewide election in Wyoming since [[2006 Wyoming gubernatorial election|2006]]. As a result of the Constitution Party getting more than 10% in this race, it will become a major party in the state.{{cite news |last1=Mullen |first1=Maggie |last2=WyoFile |title=Wyoming Is Poised to Welcome a Third Political Party |url=https://www.governing.com/politics/wyoming-is-poised-to-welcome-a-third-political-party |work=Governing |date=5 November 2026 |language=en}} This is the first time a Democratic gubernatorial candidate has not finished in the top two since Wyoming gained statehood. {{toclimit|3}} ==Republican primary== ===Candidates=== ====Nominee==== *[[Eric Barlow]], [[Wyoming Senate|state senator]] from the [[Wyoming's 23rd State Senate district|23rd district]] (2023–present){{cite web |last=Zahn |first=Noah |date=August 12, 2025 |title=Sen.
